There’s a straight swap in Leeds’ midfield as Tanaka is withdrawn for Longstaff. This game appears destined to be 0-0. Can either side find a late winner?

Leeds make the next change as Nmecha replaces Calvert-Lewin up top. Trafford collides with Muharemovic as he comes out to claim a cross. He initially stays down and it looks like he has cramp, but he’s okay to continue and play resumes.

There are appeals for a penalty as Tutierov’s deflected cross hits Tanaka’s shoulder. It’s quickly checked and cleared by VAR.

It is rare you watch a game of football for more than an hour and cannot say with clarity who has been the better of the two sides. Sunderland have had their moments and Leeds’ James Trafford has been the busier of the two. Yet, Leeds have also had periods in the game when they have looked the more threatening and it has taken some valiant last ditch defending from the home side to deny them.

There’s a double change for Sunderland as Diarra and Talbi replace Angulo and Le Fee. Can either of these substitutes help the hosts claim a victory?

A double change from RLB 🔄 https://t.co/8E2MVJYLyM

On the turn, Tanaka swivels and shoots from just outside the penalty area. Roefs spills the fierce strike and Calvert-Lewin attempts to pounce on to the rebound. The goalkeeper gets another hand to the ball, preventing the striker from a tap-in. There are cries from the Leeds support up high in the away end for a penalty, but the situation is quickly checked and cleared by VAR.

Robin Roefs produced a quick double save to deny Tanaka and Calvert-Lewin from opening the scoring for Leeds 🧤 https://t.co/9otOjISuNh

Bogle bursts forward on the right flank and fires a powerful, teasing cross towards the back post. Okafor makes the run, but Sadiki is there to make a terrific interception and clear the danger.

Sunderland take advantage of the windy conditions as Trafford flaps at Xhaka’s looped corner. The ball drops to Angulo, whose low, driven half-volley is blocked by a sea of Leeds bodies.

Le Fee tries to slide an intricate pass through to Tutierov, but it’s cut out by Bijol, who reads the situation well.

Bogle catches Reinildo above his hip with a high boot. The referee gives the Leeds man a yellow card. Sunderland want something more. That was certainly a risky tackle from Bogle, who now must be careful.

Let's go, Timur 👊 https://t.co/JVxgPM7zAC

Attacking changes are here for both sides. Brobbey’s Sunderland return lasts for over an hour and he’s replaced by Tutierov. Meanwhile, for the visitors, Wilson and Aaronson depart for Stach and Okafor.

Bogle carelessly catches Angulo with a late tackle, gifting Sunderland a great chance to swing the ball into the box. Le Fee whips it in, but its flicked on and goes out for a goal kick.

This game is now being played at a much quicker tempo, with Justin bending an effort towards the far top corner. However, it drifts wide. Both sides look far more confident now and not like they’re playing for a draw.

At the other end, the ball breaks to Angulo, who stings Trafford’s palms with a fierce curling strike that forces the Leeds goalkeeper into conceding a corner. Excitement in this second half is starting to ramp up.

Leeds come forward again as Bogle tries to slide a low cross into Tanaka, but Le Fee tracks back to prevent the visitors from getting a shot off.

Wilson whips in a deep corner. Muharemovic wins the header at the back stick, but can’t get threatening contact on it and slowly directs it into Roefs’ grasp.

If I’m being kind to the players out there, playing in a strong wind at the Stadium of Light is notoriously tricky.

If you are watching on television, you might have noticed in the first half the litter being blown around in circles on the pitch. That will give you an idea of the conditions. The wind tends to swirl around inside this stadium rather than blowing in one direction. If I were any good at physics I would be able to tell you why. But I’m not. So I can’t.

Still, this match is yet to strike an attacking rhythm. Leeds have dominated the ball since the break, with Mukiele’s injury and subsequent departure slightly unsettling the hosts. Aaronson acrobatically knocks the ball across the six-yard box, but it’s hooked clear by Sunderland.

Mukiele won’t return to the action and heads down the tunnel. Alderete is on to replace his fellow defender. That is a blow for Sunderland to lose Mukiele this early in the second half.

We're forced into a change 🔄 https://t.co/ZJB0NOnawt

Mukiele is sat up and is still receiving treatment after being caught by O’Nein on his Adam’s apple. He walks off the pitch and it’s unclear if he’s able to continue. For now, Sunderland are down to 10 men.

The medical staff are waved on to the pitch as O’Nein accidentally catches Mukiele in the face with his outstretched arm.

We are back under way for the second half. Both sides are unchanged at the break.

Only two shots on target in that first half, with Brobbey forcing a couple of saves from Trafford. Hopefully we’re treated to some more exciting football after the break.

In a game lacking creativity and chances, nothing separates Sunderland and Leeds at the break. The best chance of the first half fell to Brobbey, but Trafford did well to smother the one-on-one opportunity.

There will be just one minute of added time to end this first half.

Nearly a disaster at the back for Sunderland as O’Nein lets a ball run thinking Roefs will come out to clear. However, the goalkeeper stays put. With Calvert-Lewin closing in, O’Nein has to make a last-ditch sliding challenge to direct the ball back to Roefs to stop the striker in his tracks.

Reinildo is booked as Bogle turns him, with the Sunderland defender dragging the Leeds man to the florr. He protests his innocence, and in fairness to Reinildo, he has a ripped shirt. He must be freezing.

Hume draws huge applause from the home fans as he crunches into a challenge on Gudmundsson. The Sunderland fans loved that sliding tackle.

Leeds are still waiting to record a shot on target. They’ve been pretty safe and unadventurous in forward areas so far.

A lot of huff and puff, honest endeavour and robust challenges in this game so far, but the two moments of quality have come from Leeds United goalkeeper James Trafford. His first save to deny Brian Brobbey was excellent. He perfectly judged the trajectory of an awkward bouncing ball at full stretch, but I think the second is even better.

Trafford was in a really vulnerable position, well outside his six yard box in a one-on-one with the Netherlands international but the way he stood up and timed when to move for the ball was superb. He may have saved with his feet, but he cramped Brobbey for room and timed his moment to dive at his feet perfectly. That was elite level goalkeeping in a really tricky situation that favoured the striker.

Ampadu picks up the game’s first yellow card for bumping into Angulo on the edge of his own box. Sunderland now have a free kick in a promising position. Unfortunately for the hosts, Le Fee smacks it straight into the wall.

Sunderland’s pressure nearly pays off as Xhaka forces Wilson into a mistake. Brobbey is then too strong for Bijol and shrugs the defender off the ball. From a tight angle, the striker has a one-on-one opportunity against Trafford, but the Leeds goalkeeper does well to block Brobbey’s side-footed effort.

Sunderland fans are urging their side to press at every opportunity, cheering each time an intervention is successful. Still, we wait for the first notable chance.

Mukiele is down after being caught in the face by Calvert-Lewin as they both challenged for a high ball. There was no malice in the striker’s attempt to win possession and play swiftly continues following some quick treatment for Mukiele.

Mukiele was gearing up for a long throw, but the Sunderland defender held onto the ball for too long, with referee Attwell sounding his whistle to give possession back to Leeds.

Ampadu’s long throw-in casuses some momentary chaos in Sunderland’s six-yard box. However, the linesman’s flag is raised and Leeds’ chance disappears.

It’s been a scrappy opening to this game. Mukiele tries a very ambitious effort from long range, but he drags the shot well wide and it harmlessly trickles out of play.

O’Nein defends unconvincingly as he battles with Calvert-Lewin and attempts to deal with a long ball. The centre back just about handles the situation and prevents the striker from carving out a one-on-one opportunity.

On his return to the Sunderland line-up, Brobbey tests Trafford in Sunderland’s first attack. The striker’s deflected effort bounces awkwardly in front of the goalkeeper, who parries the ball out for a corner. Leeds then defend the set-piece well and clear the danger.

That was a deceptively hard save for James Trafford to make to deny Brian Brobbey. Although the connection was not the cleanest, that almost made it harder as the flight of the ball was difficult to pick up. The bounce just in front of the England international meant he had to watch it all the way and keep a strong hand at full stretch. Excellent work from the summer signing from Manchester City.

Leeds are dominating the ball in these early exchanges. Sunderland look slightly unsettled so far. Bogle is pushing particularly far forward for the visitors.

Wilson starts for Leeds. The Welshman was pivotal for Fulham last season. His Leeds career is yet to meaningfully get going, but he has a great chance to impress today.

Leeds get us under way here. How will come out on top in these feisty northern weather conditions?

My favourite part of every Sunderland game is the singing of Elvis Presley’ Can’t Help Falling in Love before kick off. Not sure the “The King” had a football club on Wearside in mind when he wrote it but it just works as a pre-match anthem. I also grew up in a house where there was a lot of Elivs playing when I was a small child. Anyway, on to the football.

The Stadium of Light is in fantastic spirits as per usual, despite Sunderland floundering in 20th position. Can the home side record a much-needed win to ignite their domestic season?

Starting good in the season, we are really keen to follow our goals for our system where we train every week and we follow how our team should play.

And, how the XI plus the subs should play together, fight for each other, and we have to keep on going like this. We know how good Sunderland are.

The team is good. Obviously, every team has a different start in the season but still we know what this team can do. Last year they achieved Europe so it is a really big thing.

We know the players and, yeah, we know how hard these games can be but we are here to try to win and to take all the points.

It is going to be a tough one. Also, the weather, I think. The wind is unbelievable but we are ready. We are here and ready to fight.

We go into every game confident and ready to fight for the three points. We are here to win. We are going for every game [because] we want to win so we will try our best and fight.

Right now, I think his intensity against the ball, his workload against the ball, is on a way better level in comparison to how it was when he arrived and as soon as he adapts, I’m pretty sure his quality will shine through sooner rather than later.

Leeds are always a good side, it was in the Championship and now in the Premier League.

They are doing really well, they are consistent as well. They built momentum early in the season, which is always good, so they are in a different position but anything is possible in football. We think that it is going to be a new opportunity to get better.

Sunderland were warned about “second season syndrome” and shrugged them off in the summer as they looked forward to their first European campaign for more than 50 years.

They had dismissed the gloomy pre-season predictions the previous year and had gone on to enjoy their most successful season in the top flight since the heady days of the Peter Reid era at the start of the century.

So when the “experts” told them it would be much harder this season—that they would no longer have the element of surprise and the squad would be badly stretched by the extra games in the Europa League—it was easy to ignore.

You cannot blame them. It has been a magical couple of years on Wearside where everything has gone in their favour, but reality has hit hard this season.

Sunderland are bottom of the table heading into this home game against Leeds United and have not won in the league since August.

The limp defeat at Bournemouth last weekend brought things to a head, with defender Nordi Mukiele suggesting in a post match interview that his teammates had become arrogant and had forgotten how hard they had to work last season to be successful.

There was a better performance and a decent draw away to Lech Poznan on Thursday night but Regis Le Bris’ side desperately need a win in the league.

Leeds United have been one of the story’s of the season so far and have looked dangerous in every game so far.

The return to fitness of Brian Brobbey is a big boost for Sunderland, but I don’t think any side would like to face Leeds at the moment. The home crowd will be anxious.

Régis Le Bris has made three changes to his Sunderland side.

Brian Brobbey returns to the starting line-up after recovering from a hamstring injury, while Luke O’Nien and Nilson Angulo also come into the side.

Omar Alderete and Timur Tutierov are named among the substitutes, while Kevin Danso begins a one-match suspension following his red card at Bournemouth.

Manager Daniel Farke has made three changes to his starting line-up.

Jaka Bijol replaces Nico Elvedi and starts alongside Tarik Muharemovic and James Justin. Brenden Aaronson and Harry Wilson both start in place of Anton Stach and Noah Okafor, supporting Dominic Calvert-Lewin in the Leeds United attack.

Sunderland: Roefs, Hume, Mukiele, O’Nien, Reinildo, Xhaka, Sadiki, Le Fée, Rigg, Angulo, BrobbeySubs: Ellborg, Methalie, Alderete, Diarra, Ahoka, Talbi, Fofana, Angulo, Tuterov

Leeds United: Trafford, Justin, Bijol, Muharemović, Bogle, Ampadu, Tanaka, Gudmundsson, Wilson, Aaronson, Calvert-LewinSubs: Zetterer, Bard, Longstaff, Stach, Gruev, Cresswell, Nmecha, Okafor, Bahoya

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League match between Sunderland and Leeds United at the Stadium of Light.

The final game of this gameweek sees these two Northern giants lock horns once again in a very intriguing encounter, with Sunderland especially in need of three points.

Following their opening season back in the Premier League last term, Sunderland enjoyed a historic campaign, placing seventh to qualify for European competition for the first time in 53 years. Therefore, their workload for the 2025-26 season has increased, which has caused their domestic form to suffer.

Sunderland currently find themselves bottom of the top-flight table, with just one win and four points from their opening seven league matches. They’ve lost their previous four Premier League games, but a win here could lift them out of the drop zone, depending on other results at Old Trafford and Selhurst Park.

Meanwhile, in the Europa League, it’s a completely different story. Regis Le Bris’ side are unbeaten, earning seven points from the first nine available. They drew 1-1 with Polish outfit Lech Poznan on Thursday evening, and given the relentless juggling act of domestic and European football, they’re already back in today against a very well-drilled team.

Leeds have made a solid start to the season and find themselves eighth in the Premier League, having only lost one match — a narrow 2-1 defeat to Arsenal at the Emirates earlier this month. Last time out, Daniel Farke’s side drew 1-1 with Manchester United at Elland Road, meaning they’re still searching for a first Premier League win since September 14.

Speaking in his preview, Farke said: “To win any point in this league, you always have to be on it. And you always have to be close to be perfect, especially for normal sides - not like the top two. And for that, we are very respectful. So we don’t go into the trap and think we are bigger than we are. We are just the second year back on Premier League level. And we fight for every point.”

#1261. Inter striker Bonny ruled out of Ivory Coast squad through injury

Inter striker Ange-Yoan Bonny has withdrawn from the Ivory Coast squad for the Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers after sustaining an injury during the most recent Serie A match.

They are due to play Gambia at home on Thursday November 12 and then the same team away on November 17.

Bonny had originally been called up for international duty in these two matches by coach Hervé Renard.

However, a statement from the Ivorian national team confirmed that the Inter forward sustained an injury during the 2-0 Serie A victory over Como on Sunday evening.

He has therefore withdrawn from the team, and has been replaced by SK Sturm Graz forward Oumar Diakité.

Bonny turned 23 last month and has seven senior caps for the Ivory Coast, having initially represented France at all the youth levels up to Under-21.

He made his full debut for the Elephants during the 2026 World Cup campaign.

The former Parma striker scored three goals in 14 appearances for Inter so far this season between Serie A and the Champions League.

#1260. Sir Alex Ferguson’s Verdict on Mauricio Pochettino as Man Utd Manager

If there's one name you can always count on to be courted as the potential next Manchester United manager, it's Mauricio Pochettino.

At this point, he's practically been linked with the club more than Wesley Sneijder, and in the years since Sir Alex Ferguson, almost no one has come up as often.

And speaking of Fergie, with the former Spurs and PSG coach's name floating around Old Trafford once again as Michael Carrick's future looks increasingly tenuous (or at the very least uncertain), the legendary football manager's stance on the Argentine tactician has once again resurfaced.

If these previous opinions and past quotes about Poch still prevail to this day, it seems he couldn't have given a clearer verdict.

Yes, despite being given the top job full-time six months ago following a third-place finish after Ruben Amorim's calamitous spell, Carrick now looks like he could soon become the seventh true Man United boss since SAF's two and a half decades at the helm to be sacked.

His former teammate, Ole Gunnar Solskjær, is the next longest-serving in the years since, having similarly been made permanent following an interim renaissance.

Roy Keane has made it very clear which manager he would like to see at Manchester United.

As it happens, it wasn't long after Ole was let go following 168 games between 2018 and his emotional farewell video in 2021 that the Scottish sporting icon was first reported to have given 'The Sheriff' his seal of approval.

According to the Daily Star, among several outlets reporting in October of that year, Ferguson had long been a fan of Poch and his style of play.

By all accounts, it seems little had changed by the time he joined and soon left Chelsea 'by mutual consent' after barely one full term, only a few years later in May 2024, with reports claiming that he had once again renewed his personal appeal and vouched for the then-newly-installed co-owners, INEOS, to go and get their man.

As well as labelling Pochettino 'the best manager in the Premier League' during his reign at Tottenham, Ferguson had plenty to say after facing the Argentine's Southampton team in 2013. He raved:

"For the first 30 minutes I thought we were fantastic, we played really well. But in the second half Southampton have been the best team to play here this season.

"We were fortunate to win the game. They pushed on top of us and didn't give us any time on the ball."

Apart from supposed failed attempts to tempt all three of Mourinho, Pep and Klopp into the role, you could argue there hasn't been as strong a candidate to become the next 'chosen one' since he ultimately handpicked David Moyes as his replacement way back in 2013.

Despite a few cup trophies, no one has ever quite lived up to the enormous expectations that a global franchise this size comes with - but many still feel Pochettino should at least be in the running to take a crack at it.

It's also worth noting that Sir Jim Ratcliffe himself, while not the most popular or successful since buying up part of the club, is said to be a big advocate behind the push to pursue Poch, sharing Ferie's admiration; it's therefore not hard to imagine that both still feel similarly about the 54-year-old to this day.

While the decision to stick with Carrick long-term or terminate yet another ex-player-turned-coach's contract is yet to be made, and the likelihood of which direction the board will take is still anyone's guess given how chaotic things are inside Old Trafford at the minute, there is a growing sense around the club that the problems run far deeper than just the players or the manager.

In fact, it's been there for some time, especially within the fan base — you only have to look at the latest wave of protest in green and gold balloons and tennis balls being launched onto the pitch mid-game — but it now seems more apparent than ever to those watching that serious structural change still needs to be carried out for any real progress to be made.

Would Pochettino replacing Carrick with Fergie's blessing be enough to turn the shop around after all this time, or would he just be the latest to become consumed by this mammoth of a task over in the red half of Manchester?

#1259. Sources: Man Utd Set to Sack Michael Carrick

GMS understand that Michael Carrick's Manchester United future will be decided by Sir Jim Ratcliffe tomorrow at a meeting in Monaco.

Executives including Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox are expected to present their recommendation that the former United midfielder should be removed and replaced. Mauricio Pochettino, the USMNT head coach, is a leading contender to take over.

The Red Devils sit just one point above the bottom of the Premier League table after just one win from 10 matches. Carrick's reign is expected to end after a 4-4 draw at home against Aston Villa on Sunday.

Carrick's side have won just three of 15 games in all competitions so far this season, and after failing to turn things around, the club are set to remove the former midfielder from his position.

Carrick took over as interim manager in January 2026 to replace Ruben Amorim, and led the team to an impressive 12 wins in 17 games, including victories over Man City, Arsenal, Liverpool, Chelsea, and Tottenham Hotspur.

Those wins also led the team to third place in the Premier League table, helping them qualify for the Champions League for the first time in three years.

But United started the season with a 2-0 defeat away to newly-promoted Hull City, and their only wins in all competitions have come against Ipswich Town and Azerbaijani outfit Sabah.

Speaking after the recent draw against Aston Villa, Carrick admitted he wasn't sure what the future held for him in a frosty interview with Sky Sports. It appears that decision will now be taken out of his hands.

With Carrick expected to leave, the hunt is set to be on at Old Trafford to find his replacement and help get the season back on track.

A number of names have been linked with the role in recent weeks, including the likes of Antonio Conte, Eddie Howe, Julian Nagelsmann, and Fabian Hurzeler, but GIVEMESPORT sources understand that the Brighton boss is not interested in leaving the Seagulls mid-season, and he will not replace Carrick.

Fergie has never been one to mince his words...

USMNT boss Pochettino is believed to be among the leading contenders, with a release clause in his recently signed contract. He is keen on the opportunity.

Nagelsmann and Howe are also understood to be among the contenders and would be interested in the job, but the Man Utd board are yet to make a final decision on who they want to be their next manager.

#1258. D’Aversa chosen as new Sassuolo coach after Aquilani sacked

Multiple sources are all confident Sassuolo have chosen Roberto D’Aversa as their next coach after sacking Alberto Aquilani, with a contract that runs to June 2027.

This name was already being mentioned on Sunday, just hours after the 3-0 defeat to Roma that sealed Aquilani’s fate.

Although former Turkiye national team manager Vincenzo Montella was floated by Sky Sport Italia, it was clear that D’Aversa was the only real candidate for the job.

Sportitalia, Sky Sport Italia, Fabrizio Romano and more all confirm that the club is down to the details for a new contract that will run to the end of the current campaign.

He had only been brought in over the summer for his first top flight job, replacing Fabio Grosso.

As for D’Aversa, the 51-year-old is making his return to Serie A after steering Torino away from trouble last season, when he had 12 games from February to the end of the campaign.

His other previous clubs include Parma, Sampdoria, Lecce and Empoli.

#1257. Stephen Robinson was just the latest Aberdeen manager to crash and burn... it's time to look at the club and its structure

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:30 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 17:30 EST, 9 November 2026

Across the space of two days last week, Aberdeen fans were dragged down memory lane only to emerge bruised and battered for their troubles.

Friday marked the 40th anniversary of plain old Alex Ferguson’s departure to Manchester United. It was an occasion for newspapers and TV bulletins to again recall the mind-blowing feats which led to the biggest club in Britain beating a path to Pittodrie.

Three Scottish championships, four Scottish Cups, a League Cup, the Cup Winners’ Cup and the Super Cup. The redrawing of the landscape of Scottish football.

There was something especially brutal about how those glories were juxtaposed beside the struggles of the soon-to-be former Dons boss, Stephen Robinson, 24 hours later.

After eight months of grim toil in the Granite City, the four-goal home thrashing the Northern Irishman suffered at the hands of Hibernian on Saturday blew away any lingering hope he retained of turning an increasingly desperate situation around.

A proven manager who was always simply the wrong fit for Aberdeen, Robinson will lick his wounds and come again.

Stephen Robinson is a proven manager who was always the wrong fit  for Aberdeen

But while a failure to live up to Fergie’s impossibly high standards might have done for those in Robinson’s shoes in the years which immediately followed the great man’s move to Old Trafford, no Aberdeen supporter in their right mind views things through that prism these days.

The majority of those who watched Saturday’s capitulation weren’t even born when Fergie’s Reds were running rampage throughout Europe.

They appreciate that the slayings of Real Madrid and Bayern Munich which they watched on YouTube were the highlights of a golden era for the club. One they know is not coming back.

In 2026, the expectation is more modest and hardly unreasonable. That with the fifth-highest average crowd in the country, Aberdeen should be in the top six almost every year, frequently playing in Europe most seasons and winning the odd cup. Yet, they’re miles off that right now.

While Jimmy Thelin did deliver a day in the sun by beating Celtic in the Scottish Cup final last year, that success was an anomaly. There have been just two top-six finishes in the past five years, with two ninth-placed finishes and one in tenth spot.

Given all that, it’s difficult not to recall the old wisdom about being careful what you wished for.

In Derek McInnes’ eight seasons at the club between 2013 and 2021, the team never finished below fourth and were runners-up four years on the spin. The League Cup was also secured in 2014.

A run of consistency and success which supporters had long craved was soon forgotten. McInnes’ familiarity and loyalty were eventually held against him.

Five managers later, Aberdeen appear to be as far away from reclaiming their status as one of the Scottish game’s powerhouses as they’ve ever been.

‘I think we’ve been waiting on it for four or five years,’ said Gothenburg legend Alex McLeish.

‘There’s been some signs, obviously winning the cup that year. You think that’s a wee springboard for the coming season and then it’s all kind of middle of the league, lower end of the league.’

As Robinson cleared his desk last night, even those fans who didn’t want him at the club in the first place would have been reluctant to hold him entirely responsible for the current ills.

The Northern Irishman is demonstrably a good manager. He guided St Mirren to three top-six finishes and the League Cup.

Thelin performed wonders across a long period at Elfsborg. Two years ago, he had Aberdeen sitting on top of the table.

Jim Goodwin was humiliated at Darvel, but now has buoyant Dundee United believing again.

Even Stephen Glass, a left-field choice to succeed McInnes, went on to enjoy success with Memphis 901 and as assistant to Robbie Keane at Ferencvaros.

When a club appoints one manager who doesn’t work out, it’s logical to question the individual. If five managers crash and burn, it says more about the environment and the structure they work in.

‘What is the solution?’ asked McLeish. ‘It’s definitely always down to what kind of players you’ve got.

Jimmy Thelin lifted the Scottish Cup before his Aberdeen career ended in disappointment

‘It’s trying to get a team to function together. To have forwards that you know can score, to have midfielders that can show a bit of quality, beat a man, playing one-twos, being accurate with your passing. Every bit of quality comes into it.

‘The manager will always get the worse side of it, you know, because they can’t sack 20 players.’

While it’s too late to save Robinson, the club do appear to have moved to address this particular shortcoming.

Back in March, Darren Mowbray returned to Pittodrie as head of recruitment three years on from his first stint which saw the captures of Bojan Miovski and Ylber Ramadani.

The trouble is that the mish-mash of players who were recruited by Jordan Miles, Chris Badlan and Nuno de Almeida are plainly not good enough.

Mowbray, it must be said, didn’t get too much right in the summer, either.

It’s not just the failure to sign players with the requisite pedigree and character which dismays the Aberdeen supporters.

When it was clear that Thelin’s time was up in January, the Swede was shown the door without there being a replacement waiting in the wings.

While there were legitimate reasons why Eirik Horneland couldn’t commit at that moment, the Dons’ hierarchy needed a Plan B.

Sandro Schwarz came to the Granite City for talks but nothing materialised, with Peter Leven remaining in interim charge.

With the pressure growing, Robinson – a wholly unpopular choice – was unveiled nine weeks and four days on. None of this reflected well on anyone involved.

Lutz Pfannenstiel, the sporting director, has written a book on his adventures in the game which included his recollections of the time he kept a penguin in his bath.

As Aberdeen’s hopes for the season have gone down the plughole, he’s not uttered a syllable in public.

Sporting director Lutz Pfannenstiel has had nothing to say during Aberdeen's recent troubles

With former FA bigwig Adrian Bevington now in the chief executive’s role, Pfannenstiel’s input into the recruitment of the new manager will be interesting.

And what role does Dave Cormack have to play? No one doubts the chairman’s passion for the club or his financial commitment to it.

But after seven years in the post, Pittodrie, on his watch, has acquired the unfortunate reputation of being a place where managers crash and burn. And you begin to suspect they might not be the sum total of the issues.

‘Dave Cormack is a close friend and I know he’s done everything in his power to try and get the Dons to a level,’ said McLeish. ‘We saw that Scottish Cup final victory a couple of seasons ago, but the league positions are not what Aberdeen fans expect.

‘Dave will be agonising. You know what it’s like if you get something wrong. You can’t sleep at night.

‘Dave will have been through all that kind of rigmarole as well. There’ll be a big burden on him right now.

‘He’s been stoic and he’s stood by the club. He has to have massive credit for that. It’s just about getting Aberdeen to cement their name back at the higher echelons of Scottish football.’

Alex McLeish was speaking at the announcement of William Hill as official sponsor of Walking Football Scotland. To find your nearest game visit walkingfootballscotland.org

#1255. Chivu: ‘Inter will have ups and downs, important thing is how you react’

Cristian Chivu insists Inter ‘will always have ups and downs,’ but while they stumbled against rivals Milan in the derby, ‘the important thing is how you react.’

The Nerazzurri go into the break for international duty just one point off Serie A leaders Lazio, having shaken off their Derby della Madonnina defeat to Milan with a 3-0 Champions League success away to Feyenoord and 2-0 win over Como.

The coach was in Parma today to receive an award in the city where his senior management career began in 2025.

“Seasons are long, there are always going to be ups and downs, you know that you need a lot of hard work, patience, sacrifice, and the ability to get back on your feet together,” said Chivu during the awards ceremony.

“We must do everything we can to achieve results, aware that sometimes you will slip up, but the important thing is how you react. We mustn’t get too over-excited when we win, nor fall into depression when things don’t go well.

“We’ll continue to do everything to maintain that competitiveness we need to see out a season that we feel can be strong.”

Chivu won the domestic double of the Scudetto and Coppa Italia in his first full season as a coach with Inter.

Hiring him to replace Simone Inzaghi was a gamble, considering the former defender had only 13 previous Serie A matches under his belt as a coach at Parma.

“I am grateful for the faith that Parma showed in me and was given a big responsibility to secure Serie A safety there. I’d say it went well thanks to hard work and humility.

“Coming back here is a very emotional experience, I have to admit it. This city became ‘mine’ for what I wanted to give.”

#1254. Journey to Wembley: Halifax set sights on winning more fans and climbing mountain to the Football League as their FA Cup adventure is ended by route-one Cheltenham

By IAN HERBERT AT EV CHARGER POINTS STADIUM

Published: 21:00 EST, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 18:05 EST, 9 November 2026

The FC Halifax manager John McGrath’s father-in-law is the top British mountaineer Alan Hinkes OBE and he knows that he has something of a summit of his own to scale, as he walks straight from the team bus to the pitch, set in the lee of Cheltenham’s mist-shrouded Cleeve Hill.

McGrath is all-too familiar with this setting. He brought his Buxton team here in the FA Cup's second round last season and was on the fringes of a major upset – 2-1 up at half-time – before watching the game fall away.

Cheltenham are a much stronger club, 12 months on, but our few weeks with McGrath, an Irishman who 25 years ago was playing for Aston Villa against Liverpool in the Premier League, reveal his ambition for the National League side he joined this summer.

We’re alongside him and FC Halifax on our journey to Wembley, told through all 13 rounds, following a club as far as they go and then picking up with the team who knock them out, all the way to the final.

A mist-veiled evening at Halifax’s Shay Stadium, a few weeks back, revealed much about 46-year-old McGrath. He arrives with his two-man coaching team for a Q&A with fans who, when the evening’s proceedings are finished, form a long and orderly queue to talk to him, one-on-one. The team’s four-hour drive to Southend awaits the following morning. But McGrath has no eye for the clock.

This managerial journey is one he hadn’t anticipated when, aged 32, a serious foot injury ended his long career with Burton Albion. He secured a master’s degree in broadcasting and media at Staffordshire University and had begun spots for Sky Sports and BBC local radio, yet here he is on ‘the grass’ he'd never wanted to leave.

His wife Fiona is Director of Public Realm at Islington Council and their time together is some weeks limited to a coffee at Doncaster station, near their home, when he drops her before daybreak. ‘It’s our little half an hour,’ he relates. ‘We’re ships that pass in the night.'

Cheltenham edged out FC Halifax 2-0 in front of 2,961 fans to reach round two

Cheltenham boss Steve Cotterill shakes hands with Halifax manager John McGrath

Ground staff put up the goalposts at EV Charger Points Stadium, also known as Whaddon Road

His club’s fans are partisan – 350 are here – and yearn for League Two, though there’s not a fortune at McGrath’s disposal. The club’s owner David Bosomworth was at the club when it went bust in 2008 and they say that experience left him painfully aware of the need for sustainability. Fair enough. Bosomworth has declined to speak to us. He is not at Cheltenham.

An hour out from kick-off, McGrath is handing out training vests for the warm-up as well as observing things – it’s a modest backroom team – and that defeat last season perhaps plays on his mind. ‘Cheltenham tweaked it that day and personally, I think I should have done the same,’ he says. ‘I’m a better manager, 12 months on.’

The club could badly use the £50,000 prize money that a win here would bring, not to mention the accompanying shot of exhilaration.

McGrath already belongs in the margins of the tournament’s history. He and his son, Jay, a Doncaster Rovers player, became the first father and son to play in the same team in an FA Cup game when McGrath, Mickleover Sports' player-manager for their preliminary-round win against Coventry Sphinx in 2019, fielded his 17-year-old boy.

Halifax seem up for this challenge. Their players go looking for their kit in their bus's luggage compartment before the driver has jumped out to produce the key. But Cheltenham have come a long way in the past year.

The former Burnley owner Mike Garlick bought the club 15 months ago and his investment strategy has echoes of the methods which made the Turf Moor club a Premier League side for seven out of eight years. Manager Steve Cotterill, quickly installed by Garlick, was briefly with him at Burnley.

Cheltenham fans arrive at the ground with their side riding high, fifth in League Two

Halifax fans cheer on their side but their Cup run is over - they travel to Kidderminster next Saturday in the National League

Mike Garlick bought Cheltenham last year and quickly installed Cotterill as manager

There’s an air of optimism around the place, as head groundsman Paul Gibson attends to some stray grass cuttings with a leaf blower and husband and wife team Gerry and Hannah Oldham sort the kit.

The ground staff, with their distinctive West Country burr, take enjoyment from several attempts at installing the goalposts before getting them upright. Mascot ‘Whaddney the Robin’ is limbering up for a leisurely lap of the stadium.

Garlick suggests we use Cotterill’s office as a quiet place to talk as the stadium begins to fill up. He tries calling the manager for his consent to do so but Cotterill’s phone rings out in the room.

It turns out Cotterill is receiving calls on his watch. This is a source of some humour as Cotterill eventually barrels into the office, exhibiting his usual energy. The two men clearly get on.

Extra preliminary round, August 8: Nelson 3-2 Stockport Georgians

Preliminary round, August 22: Witton Albion 1-0 Nelson

1st qualifying round, September 5: Avro 0-2 Witton Albion

2nd qualifying round, September 19: South Shields 7-0 Witton Albion

3rd qualifying round, October 3: Buxton 0-2 South Shields

4th qualifying round, October 17: Halifax 3-2 South Shields

1st round, November 7: Cheltenham Town 2-0 Halifax

Garlick looks more at home here than at Burnley. He also owns Spanish third-tier side Antequera CF and a club in Gibraltar but yearned for this kind of environment and Cheltenham, tumbling towards the EFL exit last year, badly needed help.

‘I missed English football,’ Garlick says. ‘I thought this was a club where I could make a difference and have some impact. When I came in, we had four points from nine games and were bottom of the league. It was hard work last season, but the fans seem happy for me to be here.

'Everyone who comes up to me says “thanks for helping the club,” which is nice. I never quite got that at Burnley to be honest. I’ve probably got more thanks here in 12 months than in 17 years on the board at Burnley. But that’s football isn’t it?!’

There’s been substantial investment in the training ground, a new stadium hospitality lounge, and Cotterill’s contacts have contributed to some eye-catching signings including veteran former Villa forward Andreas Weimann from Rapid Vienna.

Halifax start the game well, with wingers Ben Tollitt and Connor Douglas both flying and Conor Carty, the Irish forward who has been a revelation this season, ready to receive. Twice, they go close in the early stages. But Cotterill has a very uncomplicated route-one method in place and whip-fast striker Kirsten Otchere, on loan from Leicester City, looks lethal.

Will Flint’s string of fine interventions for Halifax is matched by the excellence of goalkeeper True Grant but Otchere crosses from the left for Jake Evans to score, left-footed.

This time McGrath does change things, adjusting the defensive line to quell Otchere’s threat after half time. Cotterill, whose colourful touchline antics include shoving his full-back out of the way when he blocks his line of view, grows concerned as Cheltenham’s attacking threat fades and Halifax dominate.

Carty nets from a Douglas’ crosses but is offside. Halifax lack the moment of class to convert superiority into goals. Substitute George Miller’s late header ended Halifax’s tournament for another year.

Halifax's Ben Tollitt battles for possession but his side cannot find a way through Cheltenham

McGrath and his Halifax players applaud the travelling supporters after their Cup exit

The Cheltenham fans flood out into suburban Whaddon Road fortified in their belief that something is building. ‘An FA Cup run is great for morale and also a massive contribution to the finances, because we’re hopefully going to strengthen again in January and the summer,’ says Garlick.

A foggy trip up the M6 awaits Halifax, though McGrath brings both a hinterland and perspective to the quest of start filling the famous old Shay Stadium once more and pushing closer to the fourth tier after 24 years away. His father-in-law was the first Briton to climb all the world's 8,000m mountains, in the Himalayan and Karakoram ranges of Nepal, Tibet and Pakistan.

‘He’s one of the best in the world,’ McGrath relates. ‘And however tough it is being a footballer or football manager, you try sitting on the side of Mount Everest for three months.

‘There’s a rumour building in our town that we play good football, that there’s goals to be seen at our stadium and a bunch of talented young men are representing the club in the right way.

'We want to get another 800 fans a week through the door and kick the club up the division and into the Football League. We think we can do that.’

READ MORE: Halifax reach first round in a beloved stadium they may soon lose

#1253. Hapless and hopeless Man Utd bring curtain down on out-of-depth Carrick

Hapless, hopeless and utterly humiliated. And that has to be that for Michael Carrick. It is surely inconceivable that he will continue any longer as Manchester United’s head coach. A proud club on its knees and a favoured son on his way out.

The former midfielder will carry the can. As managers always do. Even if the fault lines run so deep at United that it feels like they are almost irreparable. Owners – the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe – executives, players. A collective failing of monumental proportions. Although, again, it will be the manager who goes. Carrick knows it and it looked like it at the end. He knows the score, especially after this score.

More than four years ago Ralf Rangnick, the then interim manager, declared that United needed “open heart surgery”. Now there is barely a pulse.

An announcement must be imminent, with United turning to someone else in the fight against Premier League relegation. A joke? No, this abject performance against Bournemouth leaves United in 16th place, just a point above the bottom three, so the priority for the new man will be clear. Save them from the drop. They are 14 points off the top already, but forget that. It is irrelevant given their plight.

That is how far United have, once again, fallen. Fans in the Stretford End unfurled their “Standards” banner, bearing the faces of Eric Cantona, Roy Keane and Bryan Robson.

It was first revealed in December 2021 in Carrick’s final match as interim following Ole Gunnar Solskjaer’s sacking. This should be his final game again, under different, more traumatic, circumstances.

If it is, he is going out having made a stand. He dropped Bruno Fernandes for his outspoken comments, aimed directly at Carrick and his tactics, following the dismal 4-1 Champions League defeat away to Como on Wednesday.

At 2-0 down here it was telling that Carrick turned to Matheus Cunha when he substituted Youri Tielemans, who had been so terribly slow and ineffective, at half-time. Carrick did not bring on Fernandes. And he did not turn to the captain after, as he made four substitutions, including bringing on 19-year-old Shea Lacey. That said it all.

The television cameras catching Omar Berrada, the United chief executive, shaking his head in the stands as Carrick’s team gave away goals also told its own story. They have two wins from 12 in all competitions and none in eight. They have only beaten newly promoted Ipswich Town, in August, and Azerbaijan minnows Sabah this season. United were so careless it looked like they could not care less.

There was no guarantee, after Como, that Carrick would remain in charge after this game. So, losing and losing so embarrassingly – it was three, it should have been five – has to have obvious consequences. However cherished Carrick is. However much the fans excuse him. Yes, he has not been helped enough, but he has also not been good enough.

Finishing third and qualifying for the Champions League last season has proved to be the kind of bounce a new manager can achieve, after the pressure was relieved by the sacking of Ruben Amorim, rather than something more sustainable. There was always the fear that Carrick, despite his playing pedigree, might be out of his depth in this job. And so it is proving to be. Especially as he has been hung out to dry. Carrick certainly appeared resigned to his fate.

But what is he coaching? What is he trying to do with United? How does he want his team to play? Yes, there are limitations, but they are badly set up, tactically poor, and struggle to build attacks. The players are not responding, but it does not mean Carrick is blameless.

Bournemouth were not just collectively and individually better – and despite how good they are, that is some indictment of United – but better organised. They knew what they were doing, believed in it and relished it as they collected a fourth victory, and a fourth clean sheet in a row, after a slow start under Marco Rose, the new head coach. It was no shock.

The nature of the goals spoke volumes. For the first, a free-kick was needlessly conceded by Ayden Heaven, who endured a particularly difficult game, as he lunged in recklessly, forcing Evanilson to jump out of the way or risk injury.

Justin Kluivert whipped the ball in beyond the far post and it was met by Rayan, who volleyed in low and precise. The Brazilian was unmarked. Carrick protested – at what? – and the Bournemouth supporters sang “you’re getting sacked in the morning”.

What a finish from Rayan to give Bournemouth the lead! 🔥 https://t.co/9BV0G5Tqgi

The outstanding Rayan should have had a hat-trick but failed to take two chances in the second half, when he only had goalkeeper Senne Lammens to beat, after Bournemouth had already doubled their lead. It came as Leny Yoro slipped over and presented the ball straight to Adrien Truffert, who squared it for Marcus Tavernier to side-foot home. It was that ridiculously easy.

The third was the same, with Evanilson chasing down a ball forward by Tyler Adams. The striker should not have got there. But Harry Maguire, captain in Fernandes’s absence, gave up, pointing at Lammens to win it. Instead, the goalkeeper was beaten to the ball and Evanilson’s finish from an angle, arcing high into the net, was superb.

"What a finish!" 😮‍💨 Evanilson makes it 3-0 to Bournemouth with a stunning goal https://t.co/hPMR78Z3cX

“You’re going down with the City,” goaded the Bournemouth fans and it is that end of the table United need to fret about. Which means, for Carrick, it has to be over. The Stretford End sang his name. But it was out of support for him as a player, his reputation, what he represented, not what is happening now as they once again vented their anger at the owners, director of football, Jason Wilcox, and even the plans for a new stadium.

It was the same as Carrick walked down the tunnel, thumping his chest as his name was sung. Then it turned. The vitriol, frustration and anger dripped down on the players, washing them away.

This felt like a new nadir. And the need for yet another new start away to Chelsea on Saturday.

Former Tottenham defender speaking to the BBC:

Manchester United’s players were just standing there today. I did not see in their body language that they are prepared to do everything for the manager, the club or the fans to change their situation.

It’s an easy thing to say they are lacking leaders but it’s true. They just don’t have big characters. It is not something technical but if you are in a tunnel and you saw the likes of [former Man Utd defenders] Nemanja Vidic or Rio Ferdinand their body language told the opposition that they were going to have a tough afternoon.

Carrick admits he does not know if he will remain in place.

The club have a week off now, with the next match a trip to Stamford Bridge against a tasty Chelsea side, albeit one who lost to Spurs last night.

He says: “It’s a tough situation. What is next? I don’t know. I’ll always do what’s best for this football club. I don’t change that now. I love what I do. I love the responsibility. But we’ll have to wait and see.”

Carrick gives a non-answer over his choice to leave Fernandes on the bench.

He says: “There’s always times when you’re trying to make decisions that are to change the course of play and made a difference but those are the decisions we made today.”

Carrick then denies that his acknowledgement of the crowd was to say goodbye, adding: “It wasn’t a farewell from me. I’m mixed emotions, I’m feeling it for my players, they’re going through a tough spell.

“Some of it we can help, some of it the situation unravels and the boys are feeling it at the moment. Mixed emotions for the supporters to respond in that way.”

Carrick also tells Sky: “It’s really difficult to have a day like this at this football club and feel the emotion and dynamics of what it was like today.

“Not for me personally but for Manchester United. It was really mixed. I feel responsibility with the position I’m in. I’ve been at the club a long time. It hurts a lot going through this.”

Carrick potentially acknowledges that his time is up, telling Sky: “It was a strange, mixed of emotions at the end of the game. It wasn’t a nice way to end the game.

“It was a tough day for the players. We went into the game having been rocked. You can feel that. They’re really hurting and disappointed in there. It’s not a nice feeling. You have to accept it, we’re in that situation.”

Today’s United captain Harry Maguire tells Sky Sports: “It wasn’t good enough. Disappointed to give a goal away so early - another set play - and conceding first in the Premier League it makes it difficult.

“A mistake for the second makes it hard for ourselves. We didn’t perform well enough as individuals or as a team and we didn’t deserve anything from the game.

“It’s not clicking at the moment. Results are not good enough and performances in the last week not good enough. Still early in the season.

“Got to find something, question yourself, look in the mirror - that’s the most important thing - think what you can do more and what more you can contribute to the team and if we do that we’ll get somewhere.”

United players have said this for some time now. Each season they look in the mirror, and each season the supporters get the same.

Telegraph columnist Jamie Carragher thinks Carrick has had enough after that.

His emotional exit after the match suggested as much, with the former Liverpool player telling Sky: “He wants to be put out of his misery tonight.”

The fact that a mid-table team can come to Old Trafford and leave with three points is no longer a surprise.

If anything, it’s unusual when competent teams struggle against United these days.

Quite how replacing a manager changes a decade of falling short solves things, who knows?

At least the scoreline is not a surprise. Bournemouth always tend to win 3-0 at Old Trafford these days

Arne Slot underwhelmed last season, and Liverpool moved swiftly to appoint Andoni Iraola from Bournemouth.

They have defeated an impressive Brighton side 2-0 today, and you can read our report here.

Former Manchester United winger Ashley Young is scathing about the players who have succeeded him.

He told Sky Sports: “Unfortunately for Michael Carrick, it’s so disappointing. The fans are behind him and backing him and of course they are, because he’s a legend of the football club.

“But the players on the pitch showed nothing. They didn’t run, they didn’t look like a team together.

“If you looked at the difference to the Bournemouth team, you’d swap every single player for that Manchester United team. It was a poor showing.”

Extraordinary scenes at the end here. Carrick walks around the pitch waving at the fans and being applauded back. It felt very much like a manager saying goodbye. As he reached the Stretford End they start singing his song and Carrick responds by banging his chest in front of them. But as soon as the manager disappeared down the tunnel the fans instantly turned on the players trailing behind. A crescendo of sustained boos reverberate around as they target the players and make their feelings quite clear.

Picking Fernandes on the bench meant that Carrick got to snub him, but it also means that Sky get to make a point of his efforts to express himself, which does not really help the situation.

The away side now match Manchester City and Liverpool.

3 - This is the third time that Bournemouth gone 3-0 up in a Premier League game at Old Trafford (also in December 2023 and December 2024). Only Liverpool and Man City have done so as many times in the competition (3). Dreamers. https://t.co/6EO4byrwCw

Two wins, the last against Sabah in the Champions League, and the other against Ipswich Town.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Manchester United vs Bouremouth.

United enter Sunday’s clash against Bournemouth in the grip of a deepening crisis. Wednesday night’s dismal 4-1 Champions League defeat to debutants Como extended United’s’ winless run to seven matches across all competitions - their worst sequence since 2015.

With just one victory from their opening seven Premier League fixtures, United are enduring their worst start to a top-flight season since 1986-87. Head coach Michael Carrick, a multiple champion at Old Trafford during his playing days, finds his position under severe threat, with reports suggesting another defeat could seal his departure. While both of United’s wins this season have come at home, they remain winless in their last three at Old Trafford. On an individual level, Bryan Mbeumo has offered a rare bright spark, scoring four goals in seven league outings while Bruno Fernandes continues to search for form, and the captain’s recent outburst only makes the atmosphere more febrile.

In stark contrast, Bournemouth arrive in Manchester brimming with confidence. Marco Rose’s side have enjoyed a flawless start to their inaugural European campaign, sitting joint-top of the Europa League standings after a dominant 3-0 victory over Ruben Amorim’s ten-man AC Milan on Thursday. That result marked a third consecutive home win and clean sheet, with Bournemouth outscoring opponents 8-0 in that stretch. Midfielder Marcus Tavernier has been instrumental, leading the club’s scoring charts with five goals across 11 appearances.

Bournemouth will feel no trepidation visiting Old Trafford, having gone unbeaten in their last six Premier League meetings with United (two wins, four draws). With Carrick desperate for a stabilising result and Rose’s side riding high on European momentum, today’s fixture carries significant stakes for both clubs.

A product of the Hellas Verona youth academy, he was purchased by Milan for €8.4m plus bonus in February 2026, but allowed to see out the rest of that season in Serie B where he was already on loan at Catanzaro.

His current contract runs to June 2030, and the new deal would probably not add too many more years to it, but certainly represent a significant pay rise.

#1251. Harry Kane ends England’s 25-year wait for Ballon d’Or winner

“Wow, wow, wow,” Harry Kane said as he took to the stage at the London Palladium after winning the 2026 Ballon d’Or. Wow indeed. “I am speechless,” Kane added before launching into a heartfelt speech, the wobble in his voice showing just how much this meant to him.

In truth it would have been a travesty had the 33-year-old England captain – and Bayern Munich striker – not won with his family, friends and coaches all watching from the stalls at this famous old theatre. “All those years of sacrifice,” he said of his parents, Pat and Kim, his voice faltering more than ever at that moment. It was from the heart. And faltering again as he spoke about his wife and “best friend” Katie Goodland. “This is a trophy we all celebrate,” he said, talking to his children back in Bavaria. “I bring a few others [trophies] home but this one is a special one.”

Kane’s speech was as outstanding as his football. “Lastly for me it is the journey,” he said. “Learn through resilience, determination and self-belief. My journey was not easy and I had to fight my way to be the very best right now. I hope that can give you inspiration.”

So much for the “one-season wonder”. So much for the doubters who poured scorn on him. So much for those who believed he would never make it after loan spells at Leyton Orient, Millwall, Norwich City and Leicester City. With varying degrees of success.

Kate Scott, the presenter, perfectly detected the emotion and said: “You held it together. You got through it.” It showed how much it meant to Kane, who simply and quietly replied: “Yes”.

What a winner. What a player. What a role model. The award given in the city where he has scored most of his goals. But he would not have been in the running for this accolade had he not been brave enough to quit Tottenham Hotspur after 19 years and move to Germany.

Kane was the favourite. But, despite its prestige, the Ballon d’Or process is an odd one. One journalist from each of the top-100-ranked Fifa countries is given a vote, with the organisers, France Football, laying out the criteria: individual performance, collective performance and fair play. In that order. They often go for the biggest name. Not the best.

Kane’s numbers are incredible. They speak for themselves. Those numbers show he deserved to win the prize: 65 games for club and country and 73 goals. Plus eight assists (for the judging period – August 3, 2025 to July 19, 2026). That is 61 goals for Bayern and 12 for England. That is a goal less than every 72 minutes. That is beyond elite. That is world class and legendary.

Bayern Munich and England's Ballon d'Or winner doing what he does best 🎯 https://t.co/yWNburqkpg

For his club, that is 19 goals more than any other player in the top five European leagues. And the most since Cristiano Ronaldo scored 61 for Real Madrid in 2014-15. Kane won last season’s Golden Shoe by nine goals from Erling Haaland. He reached his century of Bundesliga goals last month in just 98 games, destroying Dieter Müller’s record set 49 years ago – he took 129 matches.

Kane became one of only two players in history (the other is Ronaldo) to score 20-plus goals across World Cups and European Championships and was the only one to score in two major club cup finals, including a hat-trick. Neither Kylian Mbappé nor Lamine Yamal, his closest rivals, scored in any finals.

Both gave interviews declaring why they should win the Ballon d’Or. Kane? “I don’t like talking about myself,” he said. “The 73 goals speak for themselves.” They do.

Those are the facts, but there is also the football and, yes, the conduct. Kane has scored some superb goals during that period, not least for England. Take his two goals against the Democratic Republic of Congo at the World Cup that saved his team and Thomas Tuchel from an embarrassing early exit.

The Prince of Wales, who has been FA president since 2006, congratulated Kane on “a fantastic achievement”.

“A brilliant captain, a remarkable player and someone who has given football fans across the world so many unforgettable moments,” Prince William wrote on Instagram.

Kane, the first English player since Michael Owen in 2001 to win the award, is also the ultimate team player – so fulfilling that “collective performance” criteria – and a captain who leads by example on and off the pitch. Fair play? He was last booked in January and was cautioned just three times in 68 games and not at all in any of his 13 appearances this season.

And he works hard, so very hard. Kane was in the top 10 for total distance covered at the World Cup, despite playing a game fewer than most of the others on the list. And he is often seen winning as many defensive headers in his own penalty area as attacking ones in the opposition’s.

That work extends to off the pitch, to try to maximise his ability, to do everything to be the best version of himself and to be the best. Which he has now been recognised as. And it stems from his winning mentality. Some scoffed when Kane walked into England’s press conference before the 2018 World Cup and said he could be top-scorer – but he proved them wrong.

They probably also scoffed at the notion that he would one day be declared the best player in the world and win the Ballon d’Or. But he has done all that. It confirms England’s all-time cap holder (for now jointly with Peter Shilton) and goalscorer as one of the greats. And we are privileged to witness that greatness. Wow, what a night.

By Christian FalkGermany do not have a single player among the 30 in the running to win the Ballon d’Or in London on Monday night – but Bayern Munich do have England captain Harry Kane.

For the 35-time German champions, the award is perhaps even more important than it is for the peerless striker himself. The Bayern hierarchy are planning to travel to the Palladium Theatre en masse to support Kane.

Kane is not only Bayern’s top striker, he is their international figurehead and, internally, their poster-boy professional. Club patron and honorary president Uli Hoeness described the England captain as the best signing in the club’s history. Hoeness even went so far as to say he loves Kane, and he is not alone in this.

There's only one Harry Kane. https://t.co/NfZEFmjaUN

Hoeness is one of many in the club’s leadership who have been endlessly promoting Kane to help the 33-year-old fulfil his lifelong dream of winning the trophy. Bayern officials have been campaigning on his behalf for weeks.

First up was manager Vincent Kompany, who remains in hospital for tests after collapsing at Bayern’s training ground on Friday. Kompany said: “If he can now crown his career or his season with the Ballon d’Or, that would be fitting given the way he plays for the team.”

The plaudits kept coming. Whether it was sporting director Max Eberl (“He has more than earned the Ballon d’Or. Anyone who loves football loves characters like Harry Kane”), chief executive Jan-Christian Dreesen (“One thing is clear – anyone talking about this year’s greatest individual honours cannot overlook Harry Kane”) or president Herbert Hainer (“Harry Kane embodies the idea that sporting greatness is incomplete without greatness of character. He would be a worthy World Footballer of the Year”), everyone at the club is fighting for Kane.

The official Ballon d’Or website has announced Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal as winners of the main prize in an embarrassing blunder for the organisation.

Three separate articles were published before quickly being taken down.

The headline on Kane’s article read: ‘Harry Kane wins 2026 Ballon d’Or: Here are his best and most meaningful strikes from a 61-goal season’.

The 70th Ballon d’Or ceremony takes place at the London Palladium as England and Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane aims to become the first Englishman in more than 20 years to win the award. Michael Owen was the last Englishman to win the award back in 2001.

The choice of London as the host city pays tribute to the award’s inaugural winner, England’s Stanley Matthews, who won it in 1956. This also marks the first time the ceremony will be organised outside France. Kane, who scored over 70 goals for club and country in the relevant year, is among the favourites for this year’s award alongside the likes of Barcelona and Spain’s Lamine Yamal and Real Madrid and France’s Kylian Mbappe.

Kane won the Bundesliga with Bayern Munich whereas Yamal won both La Liga and the World Cup. Yamal won the Kopa Trophy at last year’s ceremony as the best men’s young player.

Last year’s winners were Spain and Barcelona midfielder Aitana Bonmati and France and Barcelona forward Ousmane Dembele. Dembele is aiming to become just the 11th man to win the top prize at least twice, although it would appear to be very unlikely that the Frenchman will be winning the award this evening.

Selected international journalists cast their votes based on the performances of players throughout the season. The panel consists of one representative per country from the top 100 nations in the Fifa men’s world ranking and the top 50 in the women’s world ranking. Each voter ranks their top 10 candidates, with points distributed on a descending scale. They vote based on three factors: individual performance, team achievements, and class combined with fair play.

In total, 13 trophies will be presented across the men’s and women’s game, including the two man Ballon d’Or awards, the best young players and best teams. The awards take into account achievements from August 3, 2025, to July 19, 2026 (August 16 for the women).

#1250. Italy called Gatti due to Bastoni disciplinary record concern

Juventus defender Federico Gatti was a surprise late call for the Italy squad in the Nations League against France and Belgium, but it is reportedly due to concerns over Alessandro Bastoni’s disciplinary record.

The Azzurri are set to complete their Nations League Group A fixtures when facing France at San Siro on Thursday, then visiting Belgium on Sunday evening.

Coach Roberto Mancini was forced to lose Roma defender Gianluca Mancini due to injury, then called in 18-year-old Udinese talent Matteo Palma.

However, late Sunday night, he also added Gatti to the list of players attending the training camp at Coverciano.

According to Tuttomercatoweb, this is because of genuine concerns that Inter defender Bastoni will not be available for the showdown with Belgium.

There are several players in the side who are one yellow card away from suspension in the Nations League, so if they are booked against France, they won’t be able to play in Brussels.

They are Bastoni, Gianluigi Donnarumma, Niccolò Fagioli, Gianluca Scamacca and Antonio Vergara.

If Bastoni were to be suspended, then the only central defenders available would be Giorgio Scalvini, Honest Ahanor, Matteo Palma, Daniele Ghilardi and Riccardo Calafiori.

Gatti was therefore drafted in to act as insurance for some more experience in defence going into the final match.

The top two teams in Group A will go through to the Nations League quarter-final, and currently France are on 10 points, Italy seven, then Belgium six.

#1249. Toothbrush zaps bacteria with electricity that’s made when bristles move

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

The history of the manual toothbrush has been traced back to the tenth-century Tang Dynasty in China. Credit: Valentyna Yeltsova/Getty

Researchers at Peking University in Beijing have developed a toothbrush in which bacteria are destroyed not only by mechanical friction, but also through an electrical charge that is generated by brushing. The work was published in Science Advances on 4 November1.

Generating electricity through brushing is a “new twist on an old concept”, says Frank Scannapieco, a periodontist at the University at Buffalo in New York. It might reduce plaque more efficiently than do conventional manual toothbrushes, although more tests are needed to prove efficacy and safety, he says.

The researchers showed that the brush did not damage the surface of the teeth and was not toxic to human cells, but they did not look at long-term safety or cost.

Bristled toothbrushes — which humans have used in various forms since the tenth century ad — rely mainly on motion to manually disrupt plaque, the film of bacteria, saliva and food particles that forms around teeth.

The team made the bristles from polyvinylidene fluoride, a polymer that they stretched and heated to obtain a piezoelectric form — meaning that it generated a charge when deformed.

When used to scrub teeth, the bending bristles release charges that create highly reactive forms of oxygen in nearby saliva. These molecules damage the cell membranes of bacteria in the plaque, say the researchers. When the bristles relax, the material reabsorbs the charges.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03586-y

Lu, Y. et al. Sci. Adv. 12, eaeg5744 (2026).

#1248. Shea Lacey has showed the fearlessness Man United need to lift themselves out of the mire. It's time for misfiring Amad Diallo to be dropped for the teenager - and it could be the making of both players, writes NATHAN SALT

Published: 07:00 EST, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 10:59 EST, 4 November 2026

Ruben Amorim, Ruud van Nistelrooy and Michael Carrick can’t all be wrong when it comes to Amad Diallo’s unrelenting desire to fulfil his potential.

‘Amad is such a dream to work with,’ Carrick said last season. ‘His attitude is so positive. He wants to learn, he wants to keep pushing.

‘He asks for more – “what can I do more?” or “how can I improve?” He is desperate to do well and has been a huge part of the team.’

Amorim and Van Nistelrooy spoke similarly of Amad’s thirst for extra work and personal development. Nobody inside Carrington denies how much Amad wants to be great.

But there comes a point where an attacking player simply must score goals. And Amad doesn’t do that. It’s the elephant in the room that people seem uncomfortable talking about.

It is now 324 days and counting since Amad scored a goal of any kind for United, dating back to December 15, 2025, in a 4-4 draw at home to Bournemouth.

Amad Diallo struggled to make an impact against Roma on Tuesday night. It is now 324 days and counting since he last scored a goal for Man United

The best thing for Amad right now would be to take him out of the side, sit him down, and have some honest conversations as to how a player so talented has seen his trajectory plateau at 24

Go back further and, since bagging a hat-trick at Old Trafford against Southampton on January 16, 2025, the same month he was rewarded with a bumper five-year contract, Amad has managed just four goals and five assists in 43 Premier League games.

This season the docket reads no goals and one assist in all competitions, with the latter his pass to Joshua Zirkzee in Como for United’s late consolation in a 4-1 defeat.

Amad likes to do a lot of talking on Instagram – after the 3-2 win over Roma he not-so-subtly posted ‘They're petty and hateful – they'll always have something to say’ – but with Shea Lacey clipping at his heels, he needs to start doing his talking on the pitch.

Since Amad last scored against Bournemouth in December 2025, Bruno Fernandes and Bryan Mbeumo have both scored nine goals, Benjamin Sesko has 11 and Matheus Cunha, the hero against Roma, has 12.

Amad, through 24 games under Carrick, has delivered zero goals and two assists. It’s simply not good enough.

‘The best years of his career are ahead of him, and we all look forward to helping Amad to reach his immense potential and achieve success at the club in the coming seasons,’ director of football Jason Wilcox said of the winger when he penned his new contract last year.

The truth is, the best thing for Amad right now would be to take him out of the side, sit him down, and have some honest conversations as to how a player so talented has seen his trajectory plateau at 24.

Which is where Lacey, magnificent off the bench and the orchestrator of Cunha’s winning goal last night, comes into all of this.

Shea Lacey's cameo against Roma changed the game and had his boss Michael Carrick purring. 'He gave everybody a bit of a lift coming on the pitch,' said Carrick

Lacey inspired the crowd, and his team-mates. His unpredictability had Roma dazed

The 19-year-old scored earlier this season in the Carabao Cup exit to Brighton and has largely been given a watching brief since.

But back under the lights at Old Trafford against Roma, he put in a performance that not only helped take United past their Italian opponents, but one that really ought to take Lacey ahead of Amad when it comes to Carrick's thinking for the team to face Aston Villa on Sunday.

Not only because of the incisive pass to Cunha that led to the winner, but the invention, the daring, the trickery that should have won United a penalty – an inexplicable decision after Lacey was hacked down – and the rest. It was, in Carrick’s own words, a performance full of ‘mischief’.

Lacey, born in Liverpool but a United fan, is a product of the club's famed academy. He has played for England through the age groups up to Under-20s but has yet to start a League match for the Old Trafford club, his only appearance from the first whistle coming in the 3-2 Carabao Cup defeat to Brighton.

‘I'm not going too over the top, but at the same point I’m absolutely delighted for Shea,’ Carrick said. ‘We love him to bits. He's a great young man, he's desperate to do well, he's got great ability and so in terms of coming inside and finding the pass, that's not surprising.

‘He's got that little glint in his eye, he plays with a bit of mischief if you like, so he's always looking to have that.

‘I think he gave everybody a bit of a lift coming on the pitch, and it was fantastic to see. He made the most of what he had tonight.’

That’s exactly what Lacey did. He lifted the crowd, his team-mates. His unpredictability had Roma dazed. He showed a fearlessness that United badly need if they are to lift themselves out of the mire they are in right now.

‘Amad does some really good things, but it's that end product, that is what takes you to the next level,’ former United striker Wayne Rooney said on Tuesday night.

‘And the glimpses of what I've seen from Lacey when he has come on, especially this season, he has got something in there.’

Match-winner Matheus Cunha thanks Lacey after the 19-year-old set up his decisive goal

It was a cameo that injected so much hope heading into the Villa game. Lacey completed all of his attempted passes, won most of his duels, succeeded in most of his take-ons and laid on a match-winning assist, all in just 15 minutes.

Off the ball Amad does a lot that may – unfairly – get glossed over. His defending has improved considerably since playing as a wing-back under Amorim.

But Amad is playing as United’s go-to right winger and isn’t delivering goals or assists.

To help fulfil the potential of both players, it’s time to start Lacey on Sunday. In the long run, that bold call could be the making of both of them.

Diogo Dalot has revealed Manchester United’s dramatic second-half turnaround against Roma was fuelled by the realisation that their players had ‘nothing to lose’ by going for it.

United have endured an atrocious season so far, struggling in the Champions League and sitting 17th in the Premier League.

They went in 2-0 down at half-time at Old Trafford on Tuesday night but Dalot said the dressing room's acceptance that they had hit rock bottom helped their determination to put things right.

‘If you analyse it, we had nothing more to lose,’ Dalot said after United's 3-2 comeback win. ‘I mean, that's the unfortunate situation that we are in, so we just had to really go at it.

‘You could see in the first five, ten minutes (of the second half) that we were winning duels, we were on the front foot, the crowd came with us and pushed us forward. Once you create that energy inside the stadium, it's really tough for the opponents to even create a chance.

‘That's the biggest thing we need to get out of this game – that when we play like this, when we have the right attitude, when the fans really believe that we are there, we can be a very strong team.’
