#1213. Daily briefing: Toothbrush zaps bacteria to clear plaque

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

Paediatrician Annie Andrews, a Democrat, won a US Senate seat in South Carolina in a surprise victory on 3 November. Democrats had not won a Senate seat in the state since 1998.Credit: Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty

The US mid-term elections won the Democratic party power in both chambers of the US Congress, raising hopes that lawmakers will now push back against disruptions to science introduced by the administration of Republican President Donald Trump. Democratic majorities in both the House and Senate will give the party the power to craft legislation that counteracts Trump’s science agenda. But the President could still veto these bills, since Democrats don’t hold more than two-thirds of seats in either chamber. The results have also brought a wave of scientists and medical professionals into political office. “The nerds strike back,” says Shaughnessy Naughton, president of the political fundraising group 314 Action.

A new manual toothbrush can destroy bacteria by generating its own electrical charge, rather than relying on friction alone. The brush’s bristles are made from a polymer that researchers stretched and heated to obtain its piezoelectric form — meaning it generates a charge when deformed. During brushing, the bending bristles release charges that create highly reactive forms of oxygen in nearby saliva. These damage bacteria cell membranes, the team says. When the bristles relax, the material reabsorbs the charges, ready to go again.

Two new studies analysing more than 4,700 ancient human genomes have identified the possible origins of Celtic and Germanic languages and found migrations that might have dispersed their speakers around Europe. The findings could explain why Germanic languages such as English and Dutch are so widespread, whereas Celtic languages such as Welsh and Gaelic are concentrated to a few million people in northern Europe.

Three people with drug-resistant epilepsy saw the number of seizures they had per month fall by more than 90%, after gene-laden viruses were infused into their brains as part of an early-stage clinical trial. The treatment was targeted to the small patch of brain tissue responsible for each participants’ seizures. The virus carried a gene that made neurons in that area sensitive to clozapine, a drug that activates the gene therapy, which in turn helps to suppress the abnormal electrical activity associated with seizures. The participants didn’t experience any serious side effects, but long-term use of clozapine might bring cardiovascular risks and other problems, say researchers.

Reference: New England Journal of Medicine paper

A genetics lab in Shanghai has handed almost all control over to a team of robots guided by artificial-intelligence agents. The robotic arms in the ‘self-driving’ lab can operate more than 20 types of instrument, complete thousands of operations in a single project and see through experiments that involve synthesizing and sequencing DNA, among other tasks. The system, called ‘AutoDNA’, uses a simple human prompt to design and execute experiments. While it’s running, human hands are required only to refresh reagents and service hardware.

Health information distributed as part of a randomized clinical trial can unintentionally reshape social relationships, as demonstrated by a trial in rural Honduras. Researchers found that the intervention — which involved being provided with information about child and maternal health — affected people’s friendships, financial relationships and whom they went to for health advice. In villages where only a few people received the information, overall connectivity decreased, whereas it increased in places where the intervention covered the majority of households. (Nature News & Views | 6 min read)

When NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins launched on a SpaceX capsule to the International Space Station last month, she became the first Black woman to command a crewed space mission. Sian Proctor, the first Black woman to pilot a spacecraft (on a private SpaceX mission in 2021) reflects on how commercial spaceflight is increasing access and how Watkins’s accomplishment might help lead us to a future in space that reflects the people on Earth.

Space.com | 11 min read (free registration required)

Research into Parkinson’s disease has historically focussed on the brain, and the processes that lead to the death of dopamine neurons the disorder causes. But this research hasn’t yet pinpointed a genetic component of the disease in most people, leaving its underlying trigger unknown. Now, some researchers are investigating environmental factors that could contribute to disease onset, and others have found evidence that changes to proteins in the gut could precede symptoms in the brain.

This article is part of Nature Outlook: Parkinson’s disease, a supplement produced with financial support from Aspen Neuroscience, Inc.

Within a decade, humanity will know whether artificial-intelligence tools will enable “radical abundance” or “society being torn apart”, says computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton — who won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2024 for his work in developing tools for understanding the neural networks that underpin AI. (The Guardian | 5 min read)

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03596-w

Today I’m pondering the best name for a space-cleaning robot. No, this isn’t just a silly thought experiment — the UK Space Agency (UKSA) is holding a competition to name their space debris clean-up mission. The agency is calling for maximum two-word names that fit the theme of “a name inspired by keeping space clean and safe for future generations”.

The UKSA has helpfully provided some examples of the names of past missions as inspiration — and perhaps to steer people away from the joke suggestions that have topped naming polls in the UK before.

Let us know what you’d suggest, along with any feedback on this newsletter, at briefing@nature.com.

Jacob Smith, associate editor, Nature Briefing

#1200. The surprising reason women in academia do more parenting than men

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Rachel Fieldhouse is a reporter for Nature in Sydney, Australia.

Flexible working conditions often mean mothers in academia do more parenting than men. Credit: Jelena Cvetkovic/Alamy

Flexible working policies at universities that are designed to make work life easier for parents and carers can reinforce gendered parenting roles, according to a growing body of research published this year. For instance, when workplaces offer flexibility, women end up taking on a greater share of parenting than men.

Universities “have all these policies in place, and we see so many women in science” that many people assume that women can participate in work as much as men, says Cassidy Sugimoto, an information scientist at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. But “the problem is being solved with women carrying an extraordinary burden”.

Research has already established that parenthood has a greater impact on the careers of female academics than on those of men. Sugimoto and her colleagues wanted to find out how much parenting academics do, and how that affects their productivity.

They surveyed more than 10,000 parent academics with academic or non-academic partners at universities and research organizations globally1. They found that women in academia were more likely to be the lead parent and do most of the parenting. Even when women shared parenting or took a secondary role, what the authors call satellite parenting, women ended up doing more than men did when they were the satellite parent. The only task that men were consistently doing more than women was coaching their child’s sports team, says survey co-author Gemma Derrick, a meta-researcher at the University of Bristol, UK.

The team then wanted to understand why women in academia were doing more parenting. Sugimoto and her colleagues found that women used flexible working policies — such as being able to adjust their hours to work earlier or later in the day — to take on more parenting responsibilities2. In academic couples, men, however, used the option of flexibility to justify why they did not do as much parenting as their female partner. For example, some men said that their partner chose to have a more flexible career to look after children.

A female academic from the United Kingdom wrote in the survey that work flexibility meant it was easy for their partner to rely on them “always being available” to help with the kids. A academic from the United States said: “I have the flexibility to drop off, pick up kids, send them for all activities, and feed them. I have the flexibility to make up all the work time I give up during daytime at night, work till 2 a. m. or at least midnight.”

Sanjee Perera, a workforce researcher at Adelaide University in Australia, says that academia has the “illusion of flexibility” because researchers have more autonomy to fit work around parenting responsibilities. But researchers are expected to publish papers, secure external funding, supervise students, teach and attend conferences, she says. “It’s almost like an open-ended workload.”

When men in academia attempted to use flexible working to parent more, they often faced belittling comments or impacts on their careers, says Derrick. The perception of parenting as a gendered responsibility is changing over time, she says. “The question is whether it’s changing fast enough,” she adds.

Another survey3, of 26 female academics in the United Kingdom, by Guoxin Ma, a workplace equity researcher at the Royal Agricultural University in Cirencester, UK, and their colleagues reported that flexible workplace policies, such as working from home or having adjustable working hours, made it harder for women to progress their careers after having children.

Some respondents said that they were seen as less committed to work because they worked from home, finished early or were part-time, while others said that they continued working while on leave because there was no one else to do their work.

Parenting became more equal in many households during the COVID-19 pandemic, says Sugimoto. Some couples looked after their children on alternating days or in ‘shifts’, particularly if one parent had fixed working hours. Flexible working arrangements existed before the pandemic, but now ‘hybrid working’ such as the option of online teaching and meetings has became more normalized4.

#1198. Spurs win three in row for first time in 616 days to pile pressure on Sage

For the first time in 616 days, Tottenham Hotspur have won three Premier League matches in a row. Three different managers have been sacked in that time, and the mood in north London had plunged to grim lows, but finally there is a sense that something truly exciting is stirring at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

This victory over Crystal Palace was not as impressive as last week’s triumph at Chelsea, but it did not need to be. After Palace striker Jean-Philippe Mateta was sent off in the 13th minute, Spurs simply had to make their numerical advantage count. They did so with relative ease, taking complete control of possession and creating endless goalscoring opportunities.

Roberto De Zerbi’s team ended the night with 34 shots to Palace’s two and with 758 completed passes to Palace’s 149. The goals ultimately came from two defenders, Archie Gray and Jan Paul van Hecke, but there was a long list of Spurs players who might have scored here.

Spurs take the lead through an Archie Gray header! ⚪ https://t.co/qSCECkOJur

Did this defeat mark the end for Pierre Sage, the Palace manager? The Frenchman was only appointed in June but it has been a grisly start to the campaign. Palace have the worst defence in the league, have lost six of nine games and have not produced any truly encouraging performances in the Premier League.

Even in the two games Palace have won, against Fulham and Nottingham Forest, they were lucky to do so. The likes of Sean Dyche and Thomas Frank, both of whom would be strong candidates to replace Sage if Palace do pull the trigger, will no doubt have been keeping an eye on events here.

“I am really aware of the situation,” Sage said. “I don’t like this situation. [But] you can trust in me, I will never give up. I want to be the first on the pitch on Monday. I have the rage to train more. It’s not me to decide this thing [his future]. If I have one hour, I will give my best for one hour. If I have 10 years, I will give my best for 10 years.”

The decision for Palace chairman Steve Parish, then, is whether this result represented a continuation of the team’s problems or was an aberration caused by the early red card. It would be reasonable for Sage to claim this match was out of his hands from the moment Mateta lunged at Spurs captain Micky van de Ven, but such an argument might not carry much weight with Palace sitting 18th in the table.

The challenge was foolish in the extreme by Mateta, a player who was much more successful in exiting this game than he has been in his numerous attempts to leave Palace in recent transfer windows. At first glance it did not seem the worst tackle, but the replays were damning: Mateta led with his studs and made forceful contact with Van de Ven’s ankle.

It was an inexcusably brainless act, after just 13 minutes of play, and the same could be said of Palace’s defending from a right-wing corner a few minutes later. Mohammed Kudus swirled the delivery to the back post, where Gray was unmarked. Yes, Palace were defending with 10. But no, that does not justify the inability of Sage’s players to spot Gray. Even more embarrassingly, the Tottenham player was unmarked again from another corner shortly afterwards.

It was not the first time this season that Palace’s cause has been undermined by a red card. When they lost at home to Ipswich Town in September, Axel Disasi was sent off after 34 minutes. An absence of discipline? Perhaps. Sage might argue, though, that he is not responsible for his players demonstrating a lack of basic brainpower.

Jean-Philippe Mateta receives his first red card for Crystal Palace! 🟥 https://t.co/U9UYb29mbk

All of this was welcomed heartily by the Spurs fans, who celebrated Mateta’s dismissal as though it was a goal. Recent results have restored some of the enthusiasm in this corner of north London and the mood here was buoyant, even before Gray’s opener.

“Now we are playing as a team,” De Zerbi said. “Before the international break, we were playing as many good players but not as a team. We showed our maturity. We are improving.”

The second goal was always coming and it arrived in the 73rd minute, when Van Hecke attacked a wonderful cross by Mateus Fernandes. Palace goalkeeper Dean Henderson saved the first attempt but the ball dropped onto the head of Van Hecke, now seated in the six-yard box, and he happily nodded it home.

Jan Paul van Hecke doubles Spurs' lead! 👊 https://t.co/1Odkkr8wBJ

The new signings at Spurs endured a difficult first few weeks but there were more signs here that they are adjusting to De Zerbi’s system. Sandro Tonali was exceptional in midfield and teenage talent Luca Williams-Barnett also sparkled off the bench. “Tonali was unbelievable,” De Zerbi said. “We played with two players more: Tonali was double.”

Spurs face Leeds United, Ipswich Town, Sunderland and Fulham in their next four league games. The momentum could, and perhaps should, continue to build. Their optimism here contrasted sharply with the angst of Palace, and with the troubled look that was etched on Sage’s face.

“Very pleased for the performance, very tough game. You don’t know 11 [against 11] would be different game but Crystal Palace are very tough because they defend with a low block, no space and we showed we are a mature team. Maybe we could score more goals with more nastiness, but I am very happy because we created many chances. We need more goals for sure. It’s not enough, but we are improving a lot.

“I was very nervous before the game, during the game, after the red card, it’s always better playing with one player more. But today, against this team, they played with this behaviour, all behind the line of the ball, aggressive. Very tough game.”

When asked if Spurs are looking up the table, he replied: “We don’t forget the ambitions. We have to look behind what was the situation two weeks ago. In the last two years, two times 17th in the table, many games without a win in front of our fans. We have to stay focused. They are improving, increasing the level of performance.”

Speaking to Sky Sports, the Palace defender said: “Definitely was frustrating. It was one of the first tackles of the game. And we felt like we were doing well and it is unfortunate. We go again.

“The main message was don’t concede again, stay tight as a defence and try to hit them on the counter. That is the best plan when you’re down a man.

“Unfortunately, it didn’t happen today. We know what we can do as a team, as a back five, the whole unit. There were some positives in the games, but I can’t say much when you lose. We just have to go again.

“Hopefully, the next game we win. The main message is to stay together as a team. We know what we are capable of. It is staying confident and bouncing back.”

Roberto De Zerbi, the Spurs head coach, had some good news for the supporters on Friday when he said that James Maddison was fit and available despite being taken off at Stamford Bridge. “This week he didn’t work like the other players, but for tomorrow he is available and he is a special player for us. A special player because of the character and he has unique characteristics.

“For James Maddison or the players who are coming from a long injury, they have to work more than the other players, but he has already four or five weeks he is working very hard and consistently.”

While Tottenham are chasing a third successive league victory for the first time in 616 day, De Zerbi insisted there will be no complacency. “For me nothing has changed. We started this pre-season with a long project and we have to stay calm and clear in the head to work to build something better than when we came here,” he said. “One win or one defeat more, nothing will change. We have to analyse to improve the results but to improve the results we have to improve all aspects.”

Pierre Sage, the Palace manager, lightened the load after knocking Fulham out of the Carabao Cup in midweek but seemed surprised that the fans have remained so supportive. “It’s always a good sign,” he said. “I appreciate it [singing his name at Craven Cottage] very much and I can thank them but I prefer they are with the team than me alone. Because I’m the manager, but I’m not the most important part of the team, of the performance and the result. I think the players need it more than me but it’s really appreciated from me.”

Asked what he has learnt about fan sentiment from looking at social media, he said: “I think they understood what happened, why we are not perfect at the moment. We don’t care who is the most responsible for the situation. I take the responsibility. I have no problem with that. I just want people to understand what we do and why.”

Two changes from the starting line-up that took on Newcastle: captain Dean Henderson is back in goal and Oscar Mingueza replaces Anan Khalaili at right wing-back.

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League encounter between Tottenham and Crystal Palace.

Last weekend, Spurs enjoyed a historic result, beating Chelsea 2-0 at Stamford Bridge for only the second time in the league for 36 years thanks to Mike Penders’ own goal and Mathys Tel’s stunning solo strike. This result, coupled with the 3-1 victory over Coventry City in their previous home outing, means that Tottenham have won back-to-back league games and are beginning to gather some momentum under Roberto De Zerbi.

In his pre-match press conference, when asked if he’s felt a change in atmosphere after the triumph at Stamford Bridge, De Zerbi replied: “We have not achieved our goal. We want our fans to be happy, not now, at the end of the season. Now we have to push, we have to stay focused, we have to increase the spirit, the appetite to win games in a row. To do that, we have to show if we are good enough. If we are good enough on the pitch, for sure we are ready. In the head, in the mentality, we have to show, because the step of this club is to win games in a row and to be angry day by day, game by game, win by win. One time or two times are not enough.”

Palace have endured a tricky and inconsistent start to the season under their summer appointment Pierre Sage, accumulating just seven points from their opening seven league matches while shipping 17 goals. The 1-0 League Cup victory over Fulham in midweek has momentarily eased the pressure on the Frenchman, but given their newfound success in recent campaigns, fan expectations have risen, with recent performances prompting some cause for concern.

Tottenham remain without the suspended Rodrigo Bentancur, while Xavi Simons, Wilson Odobert, Lucas Bergvall, Savio, Tosin Adarabioyo and Mykhaylo Mudryk are out injured. James Maddison was substituted early in the second half at Chelsea with an apparent groin strain, but De Zerbi insists he’s available for this one. Destiny Udogie could also be involved after recovering from a knee issue.

The visitors are without the injured trio of Ismaila Sarr, Takehiro Tomiyasu and Chadi Riad, but there’s hope that Quinten Timber and Jorgen Strand Larsen are fit to be involved this evening after they both missed the Fulham victory.

Kick-off is at 17:30, with teams coming shortly.

On Saturday, AC Milan will host Inter at San Siro for the first Derby della Madonnina of the season. It's a clash between two of the most important teams in Europe and the first derby for Portuguese coach Ruben Amorim, who joined AC Milan in the summer after leaving Manchester United in January. The two clubs will play at the iconic Italian arena, but on Thursday they unveiled plans for the new stadium that will replace San Siro, which both clubs currently share. The new San Siro will be named Generali Stadium after Italian insurer Generali acquired the naming rights in a deal worth €650 million ($725 million) over 20 years.

The project is a "71,500-seat stadium designed around one of football's most iconic atmospheres, setting a new standard for the live fan experience," according to the clubs. A bold architectural vision by Foster + Partners and MANICA, bringing together Lord Norman Foster and David Manica, the two architects who previously worked on the design of London's Wembley Stadium. The new arena will feature a striking X-frame structure and a sweeping double-curved roof, conceived to become Milan's next landmark. The stadium is a "defining investment" by RedBird and Oaktree, the owners of AC Milan and Inter, respectively, to "strengthen sporting competitiveness, unlock future growth and help shape the next era of Italian football." Two seating tiers form a continuous 360-degree bowl, creating exceptional sightlines and an immersive connection between fans and pitch. At either end, the Curvas rise as single, steep walls of support, drawn forward toward the field of play with seating inclinations of up to 37 degrees to amplify both atmosphere and visual impact. At the heart of the design is a distinctive structural form, whose powerful rhythm recalls both the legacy of Italian engineering and the intricate craftsmanship of the Duomo di Milano.

#1189. Noises from Man City's dressing room suggest Elliot Anderson is being asked to play two positions at once - with Enzo Fernandez always too high and wide. JACK GAUGHAN on the £320m problem for Enzo Maresca

Published: 07:00 EST, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 11:57 EST, 9 November 2026

Manchester City spent £320million on overhauling their midfield over the summer. In doing so, they twice broke their own transfer record. This marked the most aggressive focus on a specific need since the lavish outlay on full backs nine years ago.

All signed weeks before the independent commission’s guilty verdicts were announced, Elliot Anderson, Enzo Fernandez and Ayyoub Bouaddi heralded a new era in the City engine room. More energy, vibrancy, dynamism.

Two of them were ready-made replacements for Rodri and Bernardo Silva, with Bouaddi only 18 at the time and purchased as a potential superstar after shooting to global prominence at the World Cup.

But as Enzo Maresca heads into the second international break of the season on the back of three consecutive Premier League defeats, his midfield is the primary area of concern. And has been for a while.

A big fortnight lies in store for City’s manager, whose midfield has been wide open all year. Fine when outscoring opponents – see the 5-3 victory over Sunderland – and it makes for great entertainment yet an obvious gaping chasm when the goals dry up slightly.

The balance has not felt right and Maresca, who has gently batted away persistent questions about the midfield for weeks, must know this.

Elliot Anderson is being asked to do too much and it cost City in the 3-1 defeat at Forest

While studying tapes of all three defeats over the coming days, before City come back after the internationals to host Fulham and then go to Arsenal, he needs to determine a plan moving forward and that will include some tough decisions on individuals and shapes.

Nottingham Forest could have driven a bus through the middle of the park on Saturday night, two goals from counter-attacking situations engineered between the width of the centre circle. Twice the ostensible holding midfielder Anderson tried to nick possession, beaten to it, and City were turned around.

Noises coming from the dressing room suggest that Anderson is effectively being asked to operate as both a No 6 and No 8 when picked as the deepest of the three, to go and join play high up the pitch. That is Maresca leaning into the England international’s Action Man, everything to everyone style. That also relies on somebody covering for him.

That somebody does not exist in this current setup, Fernandez always too high and wide elsewhere.

So when they lose duels as happened at the City Ground, something the manager openly bemoaned, City are not stable enough to recover.

Liam Delap's fierce finish put Forest 2-0 ahead - and City were left playing catch-up

Club analysts have sat down with Anderson to go over video clips on how best to follow these instructions to the benefit of the team. Watching him, it’s hard not to conclude that this is a quality midfielder being asked to do too much as a single deep midfielder.

Manchester City defender Marc Guehi has withdrawn from the England squad as he battles a hip injury.

Guehi came off at half time of Saturday's 3-1 defeat by Nottingham Forest, and was due to link up with Thomas Tuchel's squad in London on Monday morning.

With Nations League ties against Croatia and Spain on Thursday and Sunday, Newcastle defender Dan Burn has been called up in his place.

It will produce moments of sheer class – that lung-busting run up the right in Leipzig on Wednesday that bore hallmarks of Kevin De Bruyne, a perfect cross for Erling Haaland’s winner – while also leaving the defence exposed.

An exposed defence lends itself to a heightened chance of individual errors, plenty of those around at the moment, and it was noticeable at Forest that the opening goal came from uncertainty in possession. Josko Gvardiol made the error, eased off the ball by eventual goalscorer Jair Cunha, but the plan cannot be to have the left back with his back to goal and no viable passing options.

When Marc Guehi’s ball went into Gvardiol, Anderson was higher and wider on the right – deep in conversation with Abdukodir Khusanov about how they’d failed to move possession well enough earlier in the sequence – and Rayan Cherki was belatedly trotting back to offer himself.

Fernandez never once enters the frame, even when Cunha is in the box and subsequently wheeling away in celebration. Maresca rejected the suggestion that there is an issue with the team’s build-up on Saturday night.

As Man City look to build from the back in the third minute, Anderson (No 5) is busy delivering instructions to Khusanov (out of shot)...

... it means that when Guehi plays the ball to Gvardiol, he has his back to goal and nobody in midfield to pass to - and is already under pressure

... and with no support, three Forest players swarm and Jair Cunha dispossesses him, leading to him scoring the opening goal

What is clear though is that there is not yet that balance, that this is not yet a unit. Maresca moved to include Bouaddi with Anderson and Fernandez against Brighton – a one-goal defeat – but that acted as detrimental to creativity. If nothing else, Brighton proved that City require either Cherki or Phil Foden on the pitch at all times.

Over the past two games, Fernandez has lurked more menacingly at the back post, offering an additional goal threat rather than just relying on Haaland. That ghosting late run saw him score in Leipzig but for a joint-British record £125million needs to offer so much more. There will be growing calls for Bouaddi’s inclusion as a genuine deep-lying midfielder but it’s unlikely that the teenager can manage the league’s physicality as a single pivot.

The Moroccan has more chance of stamping his authority when alongside somebody else, dovetailing with an Anderson as a two. That leaves Fernandez, whose barnstorming league debut at Old Trafford feels like a long time ago now.

To persist with him, he either dislodges Cherki as the No10 on the promise of far more goals or Maresca drops him back into a more conventional role that allows Anderson to flourish properly.

Something has to give because the unevenness of City’s three is giving the rest of the team uncomfortable jitters.

#1187. Manchester City might decry the 'Red Cartel' of Arsenal, Liverpool, and Manchester United, but is it real?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

As two of their number face off at Anfield on Sunday afternoon, this would seem to be a good time to find yourself one of the so-called Red Cartel. Manchester City are facing the prospect of sanctions that would cast them out from the Premier League's inner circle, while those other big-six clubs that play in white and blue have spent half a decade retreating from the title race (as, it should be noted, have Manchester United).

If City's sanctions land this season, it could be that Liverpool are the nearest rivals to Arsenal in the title race, another domestic crown carved up by the grand old dukes of the English game. Believe City's defenders and this triopoly is just what Abu Dhabi protected the Premier League from. "A conspiracy by the Red Cartel to keep clubs like Manchester City out of sitting at the top table," was how one supporter described the finding that City had breached 114 of the Premier League's rules over a nine-season period. When their chief executive Ferran Soriano talks about a "Premier League conspiracy theory," well, no one thinks the shadowy cabal is being led by Brentford and Bournemouth.

A version of this framing has gathered pace beyond the realms of the Etihad Stadium, intermingling with burgeoning dissatisfaction over financial rules from both the Premier League and UEFA, that have resulted in sanctions for grand old clubs such as Everton, Nottingham Forest and Aston Villa. It was best articulated by ex-Chelsea midfielder Joe Cole earlier this month, who insisted that the game's financial settlement was locking out ambitious clubs in a way that his former club was not when it was bought by Roman Abramovich.

"The regulations that are in place are not doing the job they're supposed to do," he said. Of course, there is one crucial caveat to any assessment of the Premier League's profit and sustainability regulations (PSR) and the squad cost ratio that has replaced it. When one team is found to have flouted them through "sham" contracts that inflated its revenue to the tune of over $1 billion, it is quite hard to know how this sport might operate on a level playing field. Under Pep Guardiola, City's domestic achievements were unprecedented. No English side had sustained a four-year spell of domestic preeminence, won all three domestic trophies or delivered a 100-point season.

Anyone who argues that, were it not for City, this would have been a Premier League dominated by the big boys in red must accept that they are engaged in historical counterfactuals. What actually happened was a record-breaking spell of dominance by a team that, it was found, "systematically broke Premier League rules for nearly a decade."

Then again, if you were to journey through the what-ifs, maybes and never-weres of the last 18 years, you would struggle to immediately and convincingly argue that it was City and City alone who stood against the LaLiga-fication of the Premier League. Indeed, there was never really a period when all three of Arsenal, Liverpool and Manchester United were in the chasing pack. The last season in which these teams all finished in the Premier League top four was 2008-09, the campaign whose defining moment was the unheralded sale of City to Sheikh Mansour on Sept. 1. Indeed, 2026-27 should be considered a banner year in the smoke-filled, oak-clad boardrooms of the cartel. For the first time since 2009-10, all three of their teams are playing in the Champions League. The intervening 17 years had their ups and downs for all three: a pair of eighth-placed finishes each for Arsenal and Liverpool, that 15th place for Manchester United and whatever they have themselves on course for this time out. One or two have generally been there or thereabouts, but all three at once just has not happened. Nor did it really happen before the Manchester City takeover.

The period between 1996 and 2009 is the exception to the rule, containing 10 of the 11 seasons in which Arsenal, Liverpool and Manchester United have all occupied top-four positions. Either side of that, you have broad similarities. The late 1950s and early 1960s is the only period in English footballing history when none of the triumvirate was in the top four, and the turn of the millennium the only one when all three were.

The mid-2000s was also perhaps the era when the Premier League's most successful sides had the most meaningful financial heft when compared to the rest of the English game. In the year before the takeover at what was then the City of Manchester Stadium, Manchester United posted revenues of €324.8 million, making them the second-richest club in Europe behind Real Madrid.

At that time, the seventh-richest club in England was, ironically, Manchester City. Their €104 million in earnings was barely enough to place them in the Deloitte Money League outright. In 20th place, they were being out-earned not only by the boys in red but also by the likes of Fenerbahce, VfB Stuttgart and Olympique de Marseille. The gap between them and England's monied elite was vast, United raking in more than three times the revenue of their noisy neighbors.

Move on to the most recent Money League and the picture has changed more significantly than it might initially appear. In 2024-25, the richest club in England still played in red, Liverpool taking in €836.1 million in their title-winning season. This time, however, the seventh-richest English side, Aston Villa, had earned €450.2 million.

In absolute terms, of course, the gap is far greater, but what matters more is the proportions. In 2008, the seventh-richest team in England earned less than a third of what the richest did. Seventeen years later, the richest earns less than double. Meanwhile, the comparative purchasing power of any Premier League side has risen. Nine of the 20 richest clubs in the game are English, as are half of the top 30. Two decades ago, it would have been unimaginable that a club like Brentford might snare Mamadou Sangare from the runners-up in Ligue 1, that Bournemouth might pick up future stars like Junior Kroupi and Antonio Silva, and that a newly promoted side like Ipswich might have the finances to land a Bundesliga champion in Exequiel Palacios.

As football finance expert Kieran Maguire puts it, "the Premier League is the Super League." Scarcely a week goes by without it being impressed on Manchester United that they cannot spend their way out of their latest crisis. It is perhaps too early to be certain what this all means, but it is worth noting that in the past four seasons Bournemouth, Aston Villa, Newcastle (unable to turn on the money taps like City were when they were taken over by sovereign wealth) and Brighton have all broken into the top six. If the gravitational pull of talent to the Premier League remains as is, an era of relative competitiveness seems plausible. Meanwhile, supporters of West Ham, Villa and Crystal Palace are discovering that a domestic cup win or a strong Premier League campaign can be parlayed into the sorts of European nights they will never forget.

This is not the 1950s or 1960s anymore, when provincial clubs from across the land could take a big swing at a title, but imagine a world where the regulations that Cole and others bemoan were struck from the books. Nothing would stand in the way of those with sovereign-wealth money -- Newcastle United and Manchester City -- but themselves. Those other ambitious clubs that just want to spend their owners' cash could soon find themselves dicing with danger. PSR and UEFA's financial fair play regulations would appear to have entrenched the old powers, but in the last decade and a half no Premier League side with dreams of grandeur has taken the route to the precipice of oblivion that Leeds United and Portsmouth did.

The arc of the Premier League itself might be very slowly bending toward parity, but that does not mean that Manchester United, Liverpool and Arsenal are necessarily happy with the status quo. Indeed, if there is any justification for the conspiratorial thinking of City supporters, it comes in how their rivals have attempted to change the playing field to suit their needs.

In October 2020, the owners of Liverpool and Manchester United proposed Project Big Picture, offering the lower leagues a financial life raft in the form of an immediate $325 million payment and a 25% cut of future Premier League TV deals. That came with strings attached, the most notable being a shrinking of the calendar that would surely have suited those teams with lucrative Champions League fixtures and preseason tours. Nine clubs would also have been afforded special voting rights, Liverpool, Manchester United, Arsenal (and City) among them.

A little over six months later came proposals for a European Super League. Chelsea, Manchester City and Tottenham were in on this one, but it was notable that three of the league's five founders were Joel Glazer (co-owner of Manchester United), John W. Henry (owner of Liverpool) and Stan Kroenke (owner of Arsenal).

"There has been a broad attempt to change the landscape," says Maguire. "Kroenke, Henry and the Glazers are likely to have broadly similar views to each other. Conceptually there is no doubt that what they would like from football going forwards [is greater influence and revenue]. Spurs would like to be at the table with them. Chelsea under Clearlake Capital, the same. Under Abramovich, I'm not sure it would be the same.

"Manchester City were quite happy being Manchester City. They were quite prepared to achieve what they wanted to independently, as we now find, through sham contracts."

If that all sounds quite cartel-ish, Maguire would suggest otherwise. "A cartel stops everybody else from taking part. This is an interest group who have common interest. They're trying to hijack the legacy sport of football for their own ends."

Their past wheezes may have fallen foul of the English supporter, but Maguire predicts they will try again, pointing to the increasingly likely re-election of Gianni Infantino as FIFA president next March. That could mean a doubling down on the Club World Cup, for which a joint venture has been agreed with European Football Clubs. It is expected that the 2029 iteration of the competition will make room for more clubs per country, opening the door for at least some of the Premier League's red brigade (unfortunately for Manchester United, qualifying for any global competition on sporting merit seems a long shot).

"Those clubs will want to ensure that they're at the top [of the] table because Chelsea made £80 million from winning a competition last year that nobody watched," says Maguire. "They will watch if we've got four Spanish teams, four English teams and so on as opposed to the two of the latter. It would have helped if it had been Manchester United and Liverpool, as opposed to Chelsea and Manchester City. The media interest would have been there.

"It's Manchester United, Arsenal and Liverpool that drive viewing figures, that drive clicks, that drive interest, that drive engagement."

And that is the fundamental truth that drives so much frustration at Manchester United, Arsenal and Liverpool from City in particular, but also from those across the Premier League who share Cole's view. There may not be a Red Cartel, but it is hard to argue against the fact that those three teams are a bit different. Anyone who has worked in football media will be able to tell you that there is the web traffic generated by those teams and then, a chasm later, there is the rest of the league. You might not need that expertise either. Wherever in the world you are reading this, there is a fair chance you are more likely to cross paths with an Arsenal, Liverpool or Man United fan than a fan of any other team, with Chelsea as a potential exception.

That much is apparent in Brand Finance's most recent assessment of the value of the world's top 50 football clubs. One might reasonably assume that City's perceived value to non-UAE sponsors has taken something of a kicking over the course of the last month. If that is the case, quite the gap has emerged between England's premium brands and the rest.

Ultimately, these three clubs timed their ascent fortunately. Liverpool's success in the 1970s and 1980s was among the contributory factors in their popularity in continental Europe, particularly Scandinavia, as indeed it was among floating voters in the UK. The establishment of the Premier League as a global sporting mega league dovetailed with Arsene Wenger, Sir Alex Ferguson, Thierry Henry and David Beckham duking it out for titles. It's no wonder so many felt compelled to pick a side in that great rivalry. And once you've picked your team, you're probably stuck with it. This isn't a grocery store.

These teams aren't willing to settle for what they have. Kevin Demoff, president of team and media operations at Kroenke Sports & Entertainment, has suggested that "Arsenal can be the biggest global brand in the world." The Gunners, who have worked deliberately to situate themselves at the nexus of culture and creativity since being fully taken over by the Kroenkes in 2018, are the yardstick by which the rest of the KSE empire is assessed, Demoff added. That is a collection of sports teams that includes the Denver Nuggets, Los Angeles Rams and now the Los Angeles Angels. Against all those teams, many of them championship winners, it is the team from north London that is considered the most premium brand.

Arsenal, Liverpool and Manchester United have the weight of history in their favor. Sponsors want their reflected glow. Players dream of taking the field at the Emirates, Anfield and Old Trafford. Managers convince themselves they are the one to turn the project around. Can anything be done about that? The rest of the Premier League could drag them into a more balanced playing field in financial terms.

Maguire's pitch is a hard cap based on average player costs with a "super tax." "What the owner has to do is put the additional cash in an escrow account. If the owner walks away or if their business goes belly up then you've got three years' worth of physical cash to acclimatise to a different lifestyle." Even he acknowledges that it's a hard sell. "Liverpool aren't going to vote for it because it increases competition. Brighton aren't going to vote for it because [owner] Tony Bloom doesn't have enough money to compete with Newcastle and Aston Villa."

Proposals for an anchoring system, which would have limited spending on squad costs to five times the broadcast and prize money of the league's bottom club and might have included a salary cap, were summarily dismissed when put to a vote in November 2025. Seven clubs voted in favor of the proposals. Manchester City were among those to vote against.

Realistically, even balancing out the money only does so much. If the English top flight were to implement the sort of financial regulations more commonly associated with the NBA or NFL, Arsenal, Liverpool and Manchester United would still be the premium franchises. Their resonance, their location, their history would attract the best in much the same way as the Los Angeles Lakers or Miami Heat do. However you organize a competition, there is no escaping the fact that some teams are just bigger deals than others.

Given the opportunity to hamstring the richest teams, the Premier League, in which television revenue is still distributed more equitably than in many other major European leagues, continually chooses not to. That, of course, is the point. If ever the other 17 clubs deemed the imagined cabal to be over-mighty, they could bring it to heel swiftly under the "tyranny of the majority" that was Manchester City's issue when they were fighting the league over associated party transactions. It would seem quite a challenge to run the Premier League from the shadows when you have less than half the votes required to block any changes.

And so no, there is no Red Cartel. But then you, I and Manchester City probably knew that already.

#1185. What's wrong with Kai Havertz and can he fix it in time for Liverpool vs. Arsenal showdown

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

If last season's visit to Anfield taught Arsenal anything, it was the need for a killer in the final third to break the game open. Fail to do so and they are vulnerable to the sort of magic that bamboozled them in August of last year, even if the man who scored that brilliant free-kick winner, Dominik Szoboszlai, is a doubt for Liverpool on Sunday.

And if this game is indeed one that will be decided by what Mikel Arteta terms the "moments players," then it could scarcely have come at a worse time for the Arsenal manager. Bukayo Saka -- the Gunners' top shot taker, goal scorer and expected goals compiler -- has more than a month left on the sidelines with the thigh injury he suffered in Munich. Noni Madueke could miss the trip with an ankle injury. Christos Tzolis has returned to training but has not played for his new club in more than a month. Max Dowman, the precocious youngster whom Arteta has already entrusted with turning the tide on Merseyside, will serve the first of a three-game ban for his controversial red card.

It speaks to the depth at Arteta's disposal that, even if none of the aforementioned quartet play, there will still be game changers in the side. Even so, this does feel like an occasion where a first-choice center forward in top form would be handy. Kai Havertz is not that. Twelve games in and this has been perhaps the weirdest season of all since this esoteric forward landed on English soil in 2020. At his best, he has blown his former club Chelsea away. His worst, meanwhile, includes a wasteful performance in the EFL Cup defeat at Fleetwood and a baffling new tendency to slip offside.

The obvious answer when a player slides from peak to trough in a matter of weeks is to consult his injury record. Havertz did return from the last international break early after straining a muscle and went straight back into the side, playing an hour against Leeds and featuring in every other game since. In those six games he has no goals and one assist. In most of the minutes he has played, he has struggled to link the Arsenal attack together the way he usually does, let alone to threaten the opposition goal. That is not, however, a hangover from his injury travails.

"There's nothing to do with that," said Arteta. "It's true that in terms of the numbers, we have dropped those numbers but he certainly had the chances as well to play."

That was the case against Fleetwood, seven shots for the German adding up to 0.72 expected goals. That sounds perfectly adequate on first pass, and there are certainly others in the Arsenal side who ought to have asked more of a League Two defense. And yet when chasing a game for 70 minutes, is it fair to ask for more than three-quarters of an xG from the senior attacker of the English champions, a man who has scored in two Champions League finals?

Wanting a bit more has been a familiar experience for both Chelsea and Arsenal during his time with them. For the Gunners, it has been over two and a half years since they discovered just how good Havertz could be for them. The shift to center forward in a 3-1 win over Sunday's opponents, Liverpool, was the start of a brilliant year leading the line. Across 37 Premier League games, the Germany international delivered 18 goals and nine assists, not Erling Haaland numbers but exceptional output for the center forward in Arteta's everyone-eats offense.

Even since that brilliant run, there have been flashes. For an hour in May's Champions League final, Havertz was as threatening an attacker as anyone in PSG colors. A few weeks earlier he had been excellent in defeat to Manchester City, not the first time he had bossed Arsenal's title rival. If Chelsea have the misfortune of running into their former star, they're probably going to get him in the mood to do some damage. Of all the attackers available to Arteta this week, Havertz is the nearest he has to a big-game hunter. Indeed, if you want to make the case against Arsenal "just signing a striker" in January (you shouldn't), a key component of your argument ought to be how few players suit this manager as well as a fully fit Havertz. It is just that, well, a fully fit Havertz has been an elusive creature. And yet if Arteta will not use injuries as justification for the current wobble, perhaps we shouldn't. And wobble this is. Through eight league games, Havertz is averaging fewer shots, goals and non-penalty xG than in any other season in his Arsenal career on a per-90 basis. The same is true when you adjust for the fact that the 27-year-old is touching the ball a bit less on average this season than last. There is one notable stat where Havertz's numbers have skyrocketed, though, and that is in offsides. In every Premier League season before this one, he was caught out behind the opposition defense on less than one occasion per 90 minutes. In most of them, he averaged around one offside per two full games played. This year, however, no one in the league matches Havertz's 10 offsides already, and the gap is not particularly close. Joint-second on seven are his teammate Bukayo Saka and Dominic Calvert-Lewin of Leeds.

Now, the sample size of minutes is still small and open to distortion. It might be that one explanation for Havertz's skyrocketing offsides is that he has played Aston Villa and their occasionally effective, invariably cavalier high line. Equally, not all of those 10 offsides are about what the defense did well or about a run that came at just the wrong moment from the center forward. Watch Havertz move a good moment too soon to collect a pass off his friend and captain Martin Odegaard before bending well wide from a promising shooting position against Villa, and you see what looks like a forward who is simply off color, nothing more and nothing less, really. Sometimes the easiest explanation is the correct one. Havertz is just a bit out of sync with both his game and that of his teammates, as his manager acknowledged on Friday.

"That kind of form and that kind of efficiency with the front players, it's very common," said Arteta. "Full trust on him and what he's doing."

The natural response, then, for Arteta would be to pick the next cab off the rank, as he did in the win over Everton where Viktor Gyokeres started. That was the Swede's best game of the season, but he still did not register a shot. Gyokeres scored against Fleetwood but took only two other shots. Per 90, he averages 0.92 shots, 16th on Arsenal, with both left backs ahead of him. The evidence of his past entanglements with elite opposition suggests that Gyokeres is not the player to turn to at Anfield.

Instead, it will be Havertz, in need of something of a jump-start to his season. While he retains the "full trust" of a manager who has never faltered in his support, there might be time enough to sniff out his best form.

It all went wrong for the hosts just after the hour mark in a match where Fulham provided more than a few scares before finding the net in unexpected fashion.

Alex Iwobi, who had been denied superbly by a Suzuki save just moments earlier, swung in a corner. Aston Villa manager, Unai Emery, is giving a full Premier League debut to Germany midfielder Leon Goretzka against Fulham this evening.

The 31-year-old joined Villa on a free transfer in the summer, but a knee injury prevented him from making an appearance off the bench until this month’s Champions League tie against Fenerbahce.

Asked what role Goretzka would have with Villa, Emery deadpanned: “The first one is to be available to play.”

Emery had also made a cryptic remark about Nicolas Jackson and Johann Manzambi in his Friday press conference. The suggestion was that they had been merely rested for Wednesday’s Carabao Cup defeat at Bournemouth.

Tonight sees a battle between two Spaniards at Villa Park as Aston Villa host Fulham. Both sides are looking to bounce back from disappointing midweeks having been knocked out of the League Cup; Aston Villa lost 3-0 at Bournemouth, while Fulham fell to a 1-0 defeat at home against Crystal Palace.

After a slow start to the season in the league, Aston Villa’s form has picked up, which includes handing Manchester City their first defeat of the season a week ago. After this evening, Aston Villa have games against Barcelona and Manchester United before the international break but Unai Emery has insisted his full focus is on this game.

“If we are thinking after the match against Fulham, then we are making a mistake and we are completely wrong,” Emery said. “We are prioritising the Premier League, and this is the message. To keep our consistency and demands means that each match is a test.”

Having failed to win any of their first six league games, Fulham have now won back-to-back Premier League games, with consecutive 1-0 wins over Hull and Coventry, which has lifted them out of the relegation zone.

“It [managing in England] is a very tough challenge but I am so happy to be here,” Alvaro Arbeloa said. “I am where I want to be and I am really enjoying my days. I want to win games and I think we are performing well but we need to improve.

“They [Aston Villa] are very compact, they defend so well and even with the ball they know what they have to do. And they have top players, and when you have a top coach with top players, normally you have a top team. I think right now he [Unai Emery] is one of the best coaches in the world. He is very, very good, he improves everything every year. It does not matter where he is coaching, he is doing an amazing job, and for me also it is a very good challenge to face him.”

In the two league meetings between these sides last season, it was one win apiece; Aston Villa won this fixture 3-1 just over a year ago before Fulham won 1-0 at Craven Cottage back in April. Team news from Villa Park to follow shortly.

To the surprise of many, Michael Carrick will continue to be in the dugout for Manchester United as they face Chelsea on Saturday. During their eight-game winless run in all competitions, United have allowed 15 goals while scoring six, and off the pitch, everything is unraveling, with players and fans alike questioning the direction of the club. United have been in this position before, and it has usually led to a change of manager and a rebuild of the club from the ground up. But what's different is that during this rut, players are publicly speaking out. While things will sometimes leak via undisclosed sources, players saying the quiet part out loud about what's going on with the club is not a good look. Defender Lisandro Martinez spoke about the need for the club to have higher standards and claimed that it's lacking ambition after a poor loss to Atletico Madrid in Champions League play, but it went from bad to worse as captain Bruno Fernandes spoke out after a humbling loss to Como, questioning the team's tactics.

Date: Saturday, Oct. 31 | Time: 8:30 a.m. ETLocation: Stamford Bridge  -- LondonTV: USA NetworkOdds: Chelsea -105; Draw +270; Manchester United +270

That led to Fernandes being benched and United failing yet again to pick up a victory. While the public view is that Fernandes will retain his captaincy, the episode has to strip away at least some of Carrick's authority within the club. "There is no decision to be made on [the captaincy]," Carrick said. "It will be Bruno. Listen, we're clear with the situation of the team and as a football club at the moment. He's an important player for this group. He has been and he will be." Ahead of a match where both teams are struggling, the slightest lack of balance could lead to yet another United loss. With no clear sign that authority lies with the manager rather than the captain, especially after Carrick held meetings about the future of his job, this could get worse before it gets better. What do you do if United concede an early goal and the match goes off the rails? On the evidence we've seen, it's tough to say Carrick will be able to get the club out of that spiral, and if he can't, there's no reason why he should be the manager. On paper, while too much money was invested in the midfield instead of defense, this isn't a bad squad, but United find themselves in the relegation race only one season after qualifying for Champions League play. Even their numbers scream midtable, not doomed to relegation.

That's where the mentality of the squad comes in. It's been a persistent issue since Sir Alex Ferguson left, and it's not an issue that seems to be going away anytime soon. At times, it will lie dormant for a season during which you think United are righting the ship, only to come back at the worst time possible. Carrick is only a symptom of a larger issue at Manchester United, and the club has gone through eight permanent managers since Ferguson without sustained success. It's not for lack of spending, and even though there are questions around who is recruited, for the most part, the squads have been fine. They just can never perform to the sum of their parts.

Since Jim Ratcliffe took over, the club has been more focused on profits off the pitch than actual success on it, and that's catching up with United. Turning that around is going to be quite a challenge. Fan protests have been seen, but they aren't igniting real change, and we may be in a situation where United need a sustained spell in the bottom half of the table to lead to anything different. In short, this is already dire, and every day with Carrick at the helm delays the start of that turnaround, even if that isn't his fault. United have become a club without a direction, and that's something Chelsea can take advantage of as the Xabi Alonso era at Stamford Bridge has signs of success but needs a result to get back on the right track.

#1179. OLIVER HOLT: Man United fans' anti-Glazer walkout flopped because owners don't care - but it's not impossible to oust them. Here's what they should do instead

Published: 09:02 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 12:54 EST, 9 November 2026

The only chance I ever got at holding one of the Glazer family to account in person for what they were doing to Manchester United came in Tampa, Florida, in 2009, a few days before the Super Bowl between the Pittsburgh Steelers and the Arizona Cardinals. As interrogations go, mine was rather feeble.

I was there for the game but I noticed that, as part of the week’s build-up to it, Bryan Glazer was speaking at an NFL Kids Day. The event was held outdoors, in the grounds of the Raymond James Stadium and it was open to the media so I went along and listened to Bryan speak.

As he left, I wandered over to speak to him. Everything was relaxed until I introduced myself as an English sports journalist and asked him about his family’s stewardship of United. Glazer’s smile stiffened and then it disappeared.

He didn’t say a single word. He did not break his stride. He glanced meaningfully at a security guy, who was part of his entourage, and the security guy stepped across me and blocked my path. Glazer kept walking, climbed on to a golf buggy and was driven away.

Seventeen years down the line and few have got more out of the Glazers than that stiffened smile – although Avram Glazer did tell an audience of financiers at Deutsche Bank’s inaugural Sports Investment Conference in London recently that sports teams at United’s level are not dependent on success on the pitch for commercial power. He would say that.

That went down well among United supporters, obviously, and as United languish in the Premier League’s bottom three, one point off the foot of the table, anger against the Glazer ownership, which has cost the club more than £1billion in debt interest payments and shareholder dividends, is rising to a crescendo again.

Matheus Cunha (left) and Bruno Fernandes come to terms with another disappointing Manchester United performance after the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa at Old Trafford on Sunday

The United fans made clear what they think of their owners at Old Trafford

Anger against the Glazers has been fuelled by disenchantment with Sir Jim Ratcliffe, the minority owner, whose involvement in the football operation has deepened and widened the disillusionment of the fanbase with the people who are fiddling while United burns in decline. It is 40 years since United were in the relegation zone after more than nine games.

‘We Don’t Want A New Stadium, We Want New Owners,’ a banner in the Stretford End read. The idea of getting rid of the Glazers and Ratcliffe has become a panacea for United supporters. It is seen as the key to the club’s recovery, the key to everything, but the struggle to dislodge them faces huge obstacles.

The protests are redoubling. Old Trafford was awash with green and gold, the colours of tradition and disaffection at the club, for the chaotic draw against Aston Villa on Sunday afternoon and the stadium echoed to deafening chants calling for the Glazers to get out of United. Battalions of green and gold balloons took to the air before kick-off.

The problem is that the Glazers do not care. They run the club by remote control from Florida. They are detached. They always have been. I have watched protest marches before and seen supporters gathering at the start, outside the Tollgate pub a mile or so from the ground, in impressive numbers. They have achieved little.

It is not impossible for fans to oust or defy owners. The power of supporters was at its most inspiring when it faced down the plans of Manchester City, Chelsea, Spurs, United, Arsenal and Liverpool to join a breakaway European Super League in 2021.

In Germany, some years ago, when plans were revealed to stage Monday night games, there was widespread outrage at the idea of supporters having to travel to games after work. Dissent and disobedience followed.

Tennis balls were thrown on to pitches during games, a chorus of vuvuzelas filled the air, remote-controlled cars sped on to the playing surface. Monday night games were dropped.

Liverpool removed co-owners Tom Hicks and George Gillett in October 2010 through a combination of an independent board, a High Court legal battle, and pressure from the Royal Bank of Scotland, all underpinned by huge supporter demonstrations and campaigns against the US owners.

I once confronted Bryan Glazer over his family’s stewardship of United. His smile stiffened and then disappeared

Supporters have had enough - but how far are they willing to go to drive the Glazers out?

And on a smaller, but no less heroic, scale, Blackpool supporters staged a four-year boycott of their team’s matches, starting in 2015, that saw the average attendance at Bloomfield Road drop from 10,000 to 2,500 and was critical in the removal from the club of the much-loathed owners, the Oyston Family.

That Blackpool protest movement is the subject of a soon-to-be-aired documentary on Sky called Don’t F*** With Fans. One of the main lessons that the programme preaches is the need for unity in a fanbase if the protests are to have any chance of succeeding.

Achieving that unity has already been made harder at clubs like United because of the way the loyal supporter base is being diluted by the war on traditional season-ticket holders and the move towards attracting more day-trippers and tourists, who will spend more for the price of admission and more at the club superstore.

Some fans’ groups called for a mass walkout in the 21st minute of the United-Villa game, to mark 21 years of the Glazer ownership, but only a handful of home fans observed it. The popular YouTuber SaeedTV was one of them.

‘I did my bit,’ he posted on X as he stood outside the stadium almost alone. ‘Unfortunately fans don’t care enough. Glazers OUT INEOS OUT.’

Part of the problem the call for boycotts faces is that tourists don’t do protest. They have paid too much for their seat to walk out midway through the first half.

Many of the calls for a mass walkout also come from fans on social media, who are not match-going supporters. Fans who do go to the games are, understandably, reluctant to walk out when they have paid for their seats. They also know that if they were to give up their season tickets, the club would be delighted.

Some match-going fans started a tongue-in-cheek campaign aimed at armchair fans who have been trying to preach to them how best to get the Glazers out. ‘Turn off your television sets after 21 minutes,’ was the gist of it.

But the fact remains that unity is strength. It is the only chance supporters have of moving the dial at a club as big as United. History says a form of co-ordinated, well-orchestrated, mass-participation peaceful disobedience is the only way.

Unity is strength. It is the only chance supporters have of moving the dial at a club as big as United

Some fans’ groups called for a mass walkout in the 21st minute of the United-Villa game, to mark 21 years of the Glazer ownership, but only a handful of home fans observed it

It has to be something that affects the spectacle and, more specifically, the optics for television viewers. And it has to be something that affects them consistently.

Many Premier League clubs don’t care about match-going fans anymore but if the television product is affected, if the broadcasters become concerned, if sponsors start to think that they might actually be damaged by association with the disaffection at Manchester United, then maybe at least a little pressure would be brought to bear on an ownership group.

The odds are stacked more and more heavily against supporters who wish to effect change. But the opposition to the European Super League showed it could be done. The Blackpool fan boycott showed it could be done. Liverpool supporters’ demonstrations against Hicks and Gillett showed it could be done.

It is a question of whether the will exists. Of whether the unity exists. And of whether there are simply too many of the new breed of fan who would rather take selfies and queue for merchandise than turn the club back into an institution that cares more for trophies than revenue.

#1178. MLS reveals 2027 sprint season schedule ahead of shift to European calendar

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

While the MLS regular season has yet to come to a close, the details of the sprint season have now been released. The sprint season is a critical bridge to the league moving to a European calendar, as the 2027 season will take place under a condensed schedule in order to prepare for that. Each team will play 14 regular season matches, with one home and one away. The regular season will run from February 19, with Inter Miami and FC Cincinnati kicking things off, until Decision Day on May 8t, when there's a Hudson River Derby between New York City FC and New York Red Bulls to close out the season. With NYCFC set to open a new stadium in Queens, this should also be the final MLS game played at Yankee Stadium, which NYCFC have called home since joining the league in 2015. Truly the end of an era that went on for far too long.

Ahead of the shift, MLS wants to ensure that each week has a marquee matchup to highlight the best of what the league has to offer. There will also be another season of the Walmart Saturday Showdown and of Sunday Night Soccer, so that the biggest games of the week get their due credit. With stars from abroad such as Antoine Griezmann, Lionel Messi, Thomas Muller, and Evander pitting against young stars such as Cavan Sullivan, Julian Hall, Adri Mehmeti, and Peyton Miller, there's plenty to showcase as MLS prepares for a new era.

It’s an all-out sprint. 👀The 2027 MLS Sprint Season Schedule is here. ⬇️✏️: https://t.co/5qDlJnxjeW pic.twitter.com/71brwLBgcV

The top eight teams in each conference will qualify for the playoffs, with each round being played in a single-elimination format. That schedule is yet to be announced, but it will see a shift from the current format, where the eighth- and ninth-placed teams play a single-elimination wild card match prior to the first round being a best-of-three series. That playoff format has seen criticism due to being too long, so the sprint season does offer an opportunity to take a look at other formats ahead of a return to a standard schedule in the fall. Still, using playoffs will ensure that all five Concacaf Champions Cup spots are accounted for before the teams also return to full participation in the Lamar Hunt U.S. Open Cup

This split will help get MLS onto the same transfer market as the rest of the world. MLS doing their primary transfer window in the winter has long been an issue due to teams not being able to send players to America. It also could mean that MLS sides won't be pressured to sell their best players midseason, either with the summer transfer window being an enticing time for teams to wade in and get new players during their own preseason. The change will bring geographic challenges such as dealing with harsh winters, but those are no different from the thunderstorm and extreme heat risks that the league already faces during the summer months in such varied climates. With the shift also including teams stopping play for international breaks, it will also end the need to play without your best players available, which increases the quality in the league.

Following the conclusion of this sprint season, the 2027-28 MLS Season will kick off in July of 2027. It will then conclude with the MLS Cup playoffs, which will run until May of 2028, similarly to when most European leagues wrap up.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change recommended 1.5°C carbon reduction target, requiring powerful enforcement from major economies. China, the largest CO2 emitter, is facing severe difficulties for both variable renewable accommodation and decarbonization of hard-to-abate sectors. Hydrogen, as a critical green energy carrier bridging renewable to end-users, faces significant obstacles in real-world deployment such as costly transportation, storage and fuel-cell adoption. Affordable and coordinated hydrogen deployment plan to accelerate the carbon-neutral transition remains ambiguous. Here, we present cost-effective carbon-neutral transition pathways for entire energy economy of China emphasizing the significant role of hydrogen and derivatives as green energy carriers, considering high-resolution renewable deployments, hourly power system operations in 29 provincial regions, over 46,000 rail/road/marine/pipeline transfer routing of hydrogen derivatives, process-level fuel adoption strategies in all end-use sectors. Results show that incorporating hydrogen and derivatives can reduce the overall transition cost by $ 10.7 trillion compared with renewable and electrification pathways, achieving negative carbon abatement costs ($-6.15/ton), eliminating external oil import expenses, equivalent to over 50% of China trade surplus (2023 level)1, significantly boosting employment and economic growth. Hydrogen derivative based transition pathway offers a vital direction for affordable and secure decarbonization for China and beyond under volatile international energy markets.
